events.event_narrative: At the Comertown Turn-Off MT-5 DOT site (MTCOM), temperatures in the teens below zero and breezy winds created intermittent periods of wind chills of -40 or worse during the night of January 8th. The peak wind chill of -41 was recorded at 10:56 PM on the 8th.

For multiple sites across Daniels County, temperatures in the teens and 20s below zero and breezy winds created intermittent periods of wind chills of -40 or worse from late night of the 4th into the night of the 6th. The peak wind chill of -53 was recorded multiple times between 9:32 PM and 10:32 PM at the Navajo MT-5 DOT site (MTRED).

For multiple sites across Sheridan County, temperatures from the teens to 30s below zero and breezy winds created intermittent periods of wind chills of -40 or worse beginning as early as the morning of the 5th and lasting as long as the early morning of the 7th. The peak wind chill of -55 was recorded from 1:16 AM to 1:32 AM on the 6th at the Comertown Turn-OFF MT-5 DOT site (MTCOM).

To start February, ongoing drought conditions in Sheridan County were at (D3-Extreme) for the whole county.  On the second week, the northeastern two thirds of Sheridan County improved to (D2-Severe) conditions while the southwestern third of the county remained in (D3-Extreme) drought.  By the end of the month, the whole county had improved to (D2-Severe) conditions.

To start February, ongoing drought conditions in the northwestern tip of Daniels County was at (D2-Severe) drought, while the remainder of the county was in (D3-Extreme) conditions.  By the end of the month, all but the far southwestern corner had improved to (D2-Severe) drought, while the southwestern corner remained in (D3-Extreme) conditions.

To start February, ongoing drought conditions in Eastern Roosevelt County were at (D3-Extreme) for the entire area.  On the second week of February, the eastern edge of Eastern Roosevelt County improved to (D2-Severe) conditions while the rest of the county remained in (D3-Extreme) drought.  At the end of the month, the northeastern third of Eastern Roosevelt County improved to (D2-Severe) conditions while the southwestern two thirds of the county remained in (D3-Extreme) conditions.

At the start of February the far southern corner of Richland County was in (D2-Severe) conditions, while the remainder of the county was in (D3-Extreme) conditions.  These conditions would remain the same through the end of the month.

To start February, the northwestern third of Dawson County was in (D3-Extreme) conditions and the southeastern two thirds of Dawson County were in (D2-Severe) conditions.  These conditions would remain the same through the end of the month.
To start February, ongoing drought conditions in all of Wibaux County was at (D2-Severe) conditions. These conditions would remain the same through the end of February.

To start the month of February, all but the northern border of Prairie County was in (D2-Severe) conditions, while the northern border remained in (D3-Extreme) conditions. This would last through the end of February.

To start February, all of Western Roosevelt County was in (D3-Extreme) drought conditions. At the end of February the northeastern corner of Western Roosevelt County improved to (D2-Severe) conditions while the remaining part of Western Roosevelt County remained in (D3-Extreme) drought.
To start February, ongoing drought conditions in all of McCone County was at (D3-Extreme) conditions. These conditions would remain the same through the end of February.

To start February, ongoing drought conditions in all but the southeastern corner of Northern Valley County was in (D2-Severe) conditions, with the southeastern corner remaining in (D3-Extreme) conditions.  By the end of the month, a portion of the eastern border with Daniels County improved to (D2-Severe) conditions.  This puts most of Northern Valley County in (D2-Severe) conditions, with only the far southeastern corner in (D3-Extreme) drought.

Ongoing drought conditions in Sheridan County continued into April.  The southern quarter as well as the eastern border of Sheridan County were in (D3-Extreme) conditions, while the rest of the county remained in (D2-Severe) drought.  On the third week the far northeast corner of the county improved to (D2-Severe) drought.  On the last week of April, all but the southeast corner of Sheridan County improved to (D2-Severe) conditions, while the southeast corner remained in (D3-Extreme) drought.

To start April, ongoing drought conditions in all but the far southwestern corner were at (D2-Severe) drought, while the southwestern corner remained in (D3-Extreme) conditions. These conditions would remain the same through the end of the month.

To start April, ongoing drought conditions in Eastern Roosevelt County was in (D3-Extreme) conditions for the entire county. On the fourth week of April the far northeastern corner improved to (D2-Severe) conditions while the remainder of Eastern Roosevelt County remained in (D3-Extreme) drought.

At the start of April all of Richland County was in (D3-Extreme) conditions.  By the last week in April, the southern half of Richland County had improved to (D2-Severe) conditions while the northern half of Richland County remained in (D3-Extreme) drought.

To start April, the northwestern third of Dawson County was in (D3-Extreme) conditions and the southeastern two thirds of Dawson County were in (D2-Severe) conditions. On the last week of April all of Dawson County improved to (D2-Severe) conditions.

To start April, ongoing drought conditions Wibaux County was at (D3-Extreme) drought in the northern quarter of the county, while the southern three quarters of the county remained in (D2-Severe) conditions.  On the third week of April, all but the northern border of Wibaux County improved to (D2-Severe) drought while the northern border remained at (D3-Extreme) conditions.  By the last week of April, all but the far southeast corner of Wibaux County had improved to (D2-Severe) drought, with the far southeast corner improving to (D1-Moderate) drought conditions.

To start May, ongoing drought conditions in Sheridan County were at (D2-Severe) conditions for the entire county.  By the third week in May the eastern two thirds of Sheridan County improved to (D1-Moderate) drought, while the western third remained in (D2-Severe) drought.  At the end of May the eastern half of the county improved to (D0-Abnormally Dry) conditions while the western half improved to (D1-Moderate) drought.
To start May, ongoing drought conditions in all of Daniels County were at (D2-Severe) drought.  By the end of May, conditions in all of Daniels County had improved to (D1-Moderate) drought.

To start May, ongoing drought conditions in all of Eastern Roosevelt County was in (D2-Severe) conditions.  By the third week of May the eastern two thirds of Eastern Roosevelt County had improved to (D1-Moderate) drought, while the western third of the county remained in (D2-Severe) conditions.  By the end of the month, the eastern quarter of Eastern Roosevelt County had improved to (D0-Abnormally Dry) conditions while the western three quarters of the county improved to (D1-Moderate) drought.

At the start of May all of Richland County was in (D2-Severe) conditions.  By the third week of May all but the far western part of Richland County had improved to (D1-Moderate) drought, while the far western part remained in (D2-Severe) conditions.  By the end of May, the far eastern portion of Richland County improved to (D0-Abnormally Dry) conditions, the far western portion remained in (D2-Severe) conditions while the middle portion, making up the majority of Richland County improved to (D1-Moderate) drought.

Strong synoptic winds blew through the region during the evening hours started just after 9 pm, delaying firework displays through most northeast Montana communities.  Several small wildfires were caused by the public using fireworks during the windy conditions.  Glasgow and Hinsdale both reported fires that evening.

To start May, the northwestern two thirds of Dawson County were in (D2-Severe) conditions and the southeastern third of Dawson County was in (D1-Moderate) conditions. On the third week of May, all but the far northwest corner of Dawson County improved to (D1-Moderate) conditions while the far northwest corner remained in (D2-Severe) drought.  These conditions would remain the same through the end of May.

To start May, ongoing drought conditions Wibaux County was at (D2-Severe) drought in the far northern part of the county, while the rest of the county were in (D1-Moderate) conditions.  On the third week of May, the northwestern half of the county improved to (D1-Moderate) conditions while the southeastern half improved to (D0-Abnormally Dry) conditions.  By the end of May, the northwest and southwest corners of Wibaux County remained in (D1-Moderate) drought, while the eastern three quarters of the county improved to (D0-Abnormally Dry) conditions.

To start May, the northern quarter of Prairie County was in (D2-Severe) conditions, while the southern three quarters were in (D1-Moderate) drought. By the third week of May, all but the far northwest corner of Prairie County had improved to (D1-Moderate) drought, while the far northwest corner remained in (D2-Severe) conditions.  These conditions would remain the same through the end of the May.

To start May, all of Western Roosevelt County was in (D2-Severe) conditions.  By the end of the month the northeastern half of the county improved to (D1-Moderate) drought while the southwestern half of the county remained in (D2-Severe) conditions.

To start April, ongoing drought conditions in all of McCone County was at (D2-Severe) conditions. By the third week of May, the far southeastern corner of the county improved to (D1-Moderate) drought, while the rest of McCone County remained in (D2-Severe) conditions.  These conditions would remain the same through the end of the month.

To start May, ongoing drought conditions in all of Northern Valley County was in (D2-Severe) conditions.  By the end of May, the southwestern corner and western border of Northern Valley County remained in (D2-Severe) conditions, while the rest of Northern Valley County improved to (D1-Moderate) drought.

To start May, ongoing drought conditions in all of Central and Southern Valley County was at (D2-Severe) conditions.  By the end of May the far northeastern corner of Central and Southern Valley County improved to (D1-Moderate) drought, while the remainder of the county remained in (D2-Severe) conditions.

To start May, ongoing drought conditions were at (D2-Severe) conditions in all but the extreme southeastern corner of Garfield County, which was in (D1-Moderate) drought. These conditions would remain the same through the end of the month.

During the first week of June, drought conditions in western Richland County improved to (D1-Moderate) drought to match the rest of all but the eastern border of the county, which was in (D0-Abnormally Dry) conditions. The tornado touched down 5.5 miles southwest of Glentana at 5:47 PM MDT, moving to the northeast and directly impacting the town of Glentana at 5:53 MDT.  Several blue spruce trees were uprooted, several grain hopper bins and some garages and farm machine buildings were destroyed.  The roof from a house was blown off.  The Glentana Hall metal roof peeled off on the south side.  Multiple farm machinery equipment were damaged.  Some straight line wind damage including one dozen power poles snapped, was observed 0.5 miles south of the path of the tornado on South Glentana Road.  The tornado continued toward the northeast and lifted at 5:56 PM MDT, 2.4 miles northeast of Glentana.

At the end of October the far southwestern corner of Central and Southern Valley County (bordering Fort Peck Lake) improved to D0-Abnormally Dry. The eastern parts of the county improved to D1-Moderate, while the remaining northwestern two thirds of the county continued with D2-Severe drought conditions.

Ongoing drought conditions continued across the far southwestern corner of Western Roosevelt County which remained in D2-Severe, while the rest of the county remained in D1-Moderate.  At the end of October, the southeastern three quarters of Western Roosevelt improved to D0-Abnormally Dry, while the western border and northwestern quarter of the county improved to D1-Moderate.

Ongoing D2-Severe drought conditions continued across the far northeastern one quarter of Garfield County, while the far northern portions of Garfield County (bordering Fort Peck Lake) remained in D1-Moderate drought. The remaining portion of the northern third of Garfield County remained in D0-Abnormally Dry.  At the end of the month, all but the northeastern corner of Garfield County improved to no drought classification, while the lower half of the northeastern corner improved to D0-Abnormally Dry.  The tip of the northeastern corner improved to D1-Moderate drought.

Ongoing D2-Severe drought conditions continued across the northwestern corner of McCone County, while the remainder of the northern third of the county was in D1-Moderate drought. At the end of the month, the far northwestern corner improved to D1-Moderate drought.

A bow echo thunderstorm raked through the area destroying sheds, wiping out crops and hay fields, and causing significant loss of property.  The bow echo started producing severe wind gusts and at least 1/2 hail about 25 miles northwest of Jordan in the Brussett area and tracked east-northeast through the county.   Golf ball sized hail was reported with the winds south of the Hell Creek area.  Twenty-six families were impacted with damage to their structures, livestock and crops.   A total of 213,440 acres of rangeland, wheat and hay fields were damaged partially to totally wiped out.  Six horses and a cow had to be put down due to injuries they received during the storm.  Damage information was gathered from the Jordan Tribune, and the USDA FSA agent in the county.

While mountain snow melt helped bring up Fort Peck Lake almost 20 feet from a year prior, and provide good flows on the Milk River, below normal precipitation for the months of May and June led to some areas of Valley County to experience drought conditions.  Hay yields were significantly reduced and wheat was sparse and not as tall as it should be for this time of year.  June was the fourth driest on record for Glasgow.  The worst of the drought was along the Milk River and about 25 miles north and south of the Milk River.   When precipitation did fall, it was often quickly evaporated by strong and gusty winds.  The sub-soil moisture was not very good either according to area farmers.  The drought continued into July.

This was the deadliest tornado in Montana since 1923, and only the fourth EF-3 on record. The supercell thunderstorm developed strong rotation, and rotating wall clouds and brief funnel clouds were reported in Daniels County.  As the storm moved southeast, it intensified and a large, long-lived tornado formed.  The tornado traveled for 18 miles, mostly through rural areas, but it had devastating impacts as it hit a ranch, killing two people and injuring one.   On the morning of July 27th, 2010 two teams of NWS Glasgow staff surveyed the damage area.  The first team started in Daniels County and followed the track of the storm to the east-southeast.   The second team met with county and state officials at the site of the ranch that was most devastated.   Both teams spoke to law enforcement officials, as well as weather spotters and the public who had reports of weather and/or damage as well as those who saw the tornado.   ||The initial damage from the tornado originated about 12 miles south of Redstone.   Along the Reserve and Wanso Roads, six miles of power lines were snapped off.  Sheridan Electric was able to restore power fairly quickly to the majority of residences by the next morning.  Due to the poles being snapped, the tornado was rated an EF2 on the Enhanced Fujita Scale in this area.   This was the widest portion of the tornado track with a width of a half mile.||The tornado continued east-southeast where it encountered an abandoned farmhouse, a barn and a bridge that went across Wolf Creek on the Three Corners Road.  The bridge had the planks ripped off with damage totals coming to $100,000.  The farmhouse was blown off of the foundation, had some of the siding stripped off, and roof damage.  The barn was completely destroyed, with the west and north facing walls blown away, and the south and east facing walls intact for the most part, but flattened on the ground.  Two grain bins were destroyed, with a third still on its foundation but crushed.  They appeared to be empty.   The damage at this location was rated an EF2 on the Enhanced Fujita Scale.  The width of the tornado at this point was a quarter mile wide. ||The storm continued on its east-southeast track at a speed of about 30 mph.  The Smith Ranch was then impacted.  The ranch sits on a bit of a hill with a small stream valley from the west-northwest to just north of the property.  There are no shelter belts or terrain to block some of the winds from the tornado.  The two fatalities and one injury occurred at the Smith Ranch.  The adult fatality was trying to get into the basement.  The child fatality was in the basement and the chimney collapsed and crushed him.  The adult injury was with the child, but on the other side of the chimney in the basement. ||The tornado was rated an EF3 at the Smith Ranch, with a width of three tenths of a mile.  This was the highest rating during the life cycle of the tornado.  Along with the devastating destruction of property, there was also up to 40 cows and calves significantly injured or killed by the tornado and/or debris.  Many had severe injuries and had to be put down by a veterinarian.  ||The damage totals are estimated.   ||A formal written report is available from the NWS Glasgow office.

A private stock pond (Sage Creek/Jensen Dam) on the Sage Creek partially failed, threatening a couple of county roads before it emptied into the Musselshell River. The roads threatened or flooded were Valentine and Dovetail Roads.  The dam completely failed in April according to a report from Montana DNRC.

Snowmelt and ice jams contributed to unusually high levels on the Musselshell River. The river flooded homes and closed roads for several weeks. Persistant easterly winds and a deep loose snowpack contributed to hazardous road conditions. Road departments suspended plowing operations at times as they could not keep up with the drifting. The Opheim school was hard to remain open during this time.

Spotter located on the Musselshell River near the CMR boundary reported a large ice jam breaking his utility pole and houses in his sub division were surrounded by water. Also reported that water was running over nearby road with water at the base of his house. Several streams like the Calf Creek (3 southeast of Mosby) and South Lodge Creek (15 miles west-northwest of Sand Springs) flowed over roadways deep enough to where residents could not leave their homes.

An impressive ice jam on the Yellowstone River contained ice chunks the size of a house according to an observer. This ice jam caused damage to the Shirley pumping plant at the Buffalo Rapids District 2 Irrigation Project in Terry.

On March 14th, an ice jam on the Interstate 94 bridge near Glendive caused some low land flooding. On March 15th, West Glendive beginning a threat from the Yellowstone. On March 16th, equipment such as tractor and cars had to be moved to higher ground as the Interstate 94 bridge made the ice jamming problem much worse. On March 17th, water was flowing around an ice jam on the north side of Glendive resulting in flooding of lowland close to the river. On March 18th, Dawson County commissioners passed a resolution of emergency declaration due to the flooding.

The Jenson dam totally failed causing flash flooding downstream. Water was flowing over the Valentine Road while moving toward Blood Creek. Valentine Road was closed from the junction of the Dovetail Road to the Fergus county line. The dam was already partially failed at the spillway from mid February due to  early snowmelt.
At 1510 MST, a private dam failed and was causing flash flooding downstream on the Big Dry Creek. The high water was moving towards an ice jam and towards the town of Jordan.

On March 17th, spotters reported the middle fork of the Lodgepole Creek was flooding with water over the roads and closing roads in northwest Garfield county. Also, the Steve Forks Creek and Sand Creeks were running out of their banks causing flooding in adjacent fields. Later in the afternoon of the 17th, Garfield County Sheriff reported a couple of ice jams upstream of Jordan on the Big Dry Creek. This caused a flood threat for the town of Jordan at 0157 on March 18th, flooding parts of the town. Garfield County DES reported that one of the ice jams moved downstream. At approximately 8:27pm on May 20, a tornado struck a ranch 8 miles south of Terry on 10 Mile Road. The tornado was observed by a resident of the house on the ranch. The house itself received no damage, though it was about 150 feet away from observed damage. Significant damage occurred to 4 outbuildings on the ranch. There were no injuries and the horses on the ranch were uninjured as they were out in pasture at the time of the tornado.  The damage path was about 500 feet and the width was 200 feet. Based on the damage, the wind speed was determined to be 90 mph or a low end EF-1 tornado.
At 1244 MST, King Coulee RAWS reported a measured wind gust of 58 mph, At 1506 MST, Nashua reported sustained winds over 45 mph with sustained winds over 40 mph since 1155 MST.
McDonald's DOT sensor had sustained winds from 45 to 65 mph. The Wolf Point ASOS only reported winds between 35 to 50 mph.
The Hillside DOT sensor had sustained winds of over 40 mph with peak gusts near 60 mph. The Jordan ASOS had sustained winds over 40 mph with frequent gusts over 50 mph.
Winds at Fallon were sustained over 35 mph with a peak gust of 67 mph. A gust to 61 mph were reported at Big Sheep RAWS.

Plentywood reported sustained winds between 35 and 50 mph with a gust to 61 mph while the Crosby, ND RAWS reported a gust to 78 mph. Whiteout conditions were reported by Law Enforcement on Highway 5. Electricity was lost in Wesby with winds estimated to peak at 80 mph. This created drifts to 6 feet deep, uprooted a 300 foot tall pine tree (with a 15 to 20 inch diameter trunk) and rotated a stop sign.

Poplar RAWS reported sustained winds of 40 mph while the DOT sensor at the state line reported a gust to 75 mph before power was lost at 0430 MST April 30th. Visibility of only 10 feet and drifts of 3 to 4 feet helped cause vehicles from Bainville to the North Dakota state line get stuck or slide off of U.S. Highway 2. County Emergency Manager reported that the wind and snow combined knocked out power to an estimated 1500 customers in Eastern Roosevelt and Sheridan Counties. Also on April 30th, a box car from a freight train grabbed low hanging power lines and power poles and dragged them along, ripping up fences.

Winds were sustained at 35 to 45 mph with gusts to 60 mph for several hours. A peak gust of 75 mph was reported at the Sioux Pass DOT station. Snow amounts ranged from 2 to 8 inches, which contributed to the blizzard conditions. Power lines and trees were knocked down by the heavy/wet snow and damaging winds.

Power was lost at 0235 MST in the Lindsay area.

Beaver Hill RAWS reported winds sustained above 40 mph with a gust to 64 mph. The Beaver Hill DOT sensor reported several hours of sustained winds over 40 mph with gusts over 55 mph. No damage was reported.
A MesoWest observation reported 2 hours of sustained winds over 40 mph. The Scobey Airport (Super AWOS) recorded sustained winds winds 30 to 40 mph with gusts 40 to 50 mph for several hours.

Comertown DOT site reported a gust of 65 mph at 1358 MST. A report at 1450 MST from Wesby said 60 mph wind gusts broke large limbs and stripped leaves from trees. At 1556 MST the Crosby RAWS reported a gust to 63 mph with sustained winds at 45 mph.
The US 2 Stateline DOT sensor reported several hours of sustained winds between 30 and 40 mph with gusts over 40 mph.

A farm/ranch was significantly damaged by a tornado and damaging downburst winds.  The storm stripped trees bare, four car garages were either destroyed or damaged.  A 1000 gallon fuel tank that was filled that day was blown off it's stand.  The houses received significant damage from hail and the high winds,and the majority of the windows on the two homes were busted out by the wind and hail.  A 2x6 piece of lumber was blown and implanted into the side of one of the houses.  The majority of the damage was downstream with the storm system.  The peak gust was recorded at 86 mph before the sensor was destroyed.  Quarter size hail fell with the storm as well, wiping out nearby field.  The NWS did not receive the tornado report until a month after the event, but radar data verified the possibility of a tornado, and the property owner verified seeing a funnel cloud come from the sky prior to seeking shelter.

Some light damage consisting of tree branches down and fence damage was noted south of Lambert.  More significant damage was found about 9 miles southeast of Lambert on Rd. 115.  At this location, numerous trees were uprooted or snapped, and there was damage to homes and vehicles.  Residents reported hail up to 2.5 inches breaking windows in homes.||Major to minor crop damage was seen over a large area from 9 southeast of Lambert to Savage.  An irrigation system was destroyed just north of Savage.  There was some damage to structures in and near the town of Savage, with the most significant structural damage surveyed occurring on a ranch 6 miles west-northwest of Savage.  At this location, an attached garage was destroyed with the garage door torn off and a wall blown out.  The garage door and wall, which were blown 200 feet down wind of the house.  Also, this ranch had a grain bin torn off its foundation and blown a half mile down wind, where it was found in a mining pit.||About 4 miles of power poles were blown down or snapped along Rd. 107 west of Lambert.  Poles on the south side of the road were blown down, while those on the north side were not, even though those on the south side were thicker poles.  The poles that were blown down were a little taller than those that did not get blown down, and had cross members near the top.||In the town of Savage, numerous trees were uprooted or snapped. The cemetery at Savage had the most trees blown down.||Crop damage occurred as far south as County Road 107, with hail also being reported.  However, significant structural and tree damage was reported by the public (not surveyed) further south, without hail also being reported.  A dairy 2.4 miles west-southwest of Savage had considerable damage, including the roof. All of the debris from the dairy was blown down wind towards the south.||The perception of the residents of Savage was that they experienced a tornado.  This is a reasonable perception as the residents first received a tornado warning form the NWS, then lost power, and then experienced powerful damaging winds.  However, all of the damage surveyed flowed primarily in one direction, towards the south.  Also, the damage extended over a wide area exceeding 4 miles in width, and tornadoes are much more localized.  In fact, this wide area of damage is more significant than that produced by most tornadoes.||As all of the observed damage implied flow from the north, it was concluded that the damage was caused by a strong macroburst.  A macroburst is defined as a strong downdraft from a thunderstorm affecting a path of greater than 2.5 miles.  A macroburst forms when hail and rain aloft fall and entrain air, forming a downdraft.  As large hail has a high fall speed, strong downdrafts can develop in storms with a lot of large hail (which this storm had).  When the downdraft impacts the ground, the flow spreads out horizontally, creating strong straight line winds which radiate out from the center of the downdraft along a gust front.  The rotation of the storm can add to the downdraft effect, creating a large area of uniform wind direction.  Radar indications did not show large hail approximately south of County Road 107, which agrees with surveyed crop damage and public reports.  However, significant damage still occurred for at least several miles south of Rd. 107.  It is not unusual for gust fronts to travel considerable distances away from the storms which produce them, which evidently happened in this case.||The maximum wind speeds with this event are estimated from the resulting damage.  Uprooted and snapped hardwood trees, building damage, and broken power poles are all consistent with winds above 95 mph over a wide area, with winds up to about 110 mph for the most significant damage.||The survey team did not find any damage from a tornado at any location, though one was conclusively observed and photographed.  This is not surprising as the time the tornado was observed, when combined with radar indications of a possible tornado, place the tornado in an empty area just southwest of Fox Lake near Lambert.  A tornado in this location would not have left behind any damage for the survey team to catalog.

Peoples Creek, west of the town of Dodson, rose out of its banks on June 4th and covered the surrounding low-lying areas, including Montana Highway 8 and US Highway 2. Law enforcement officials set off a quarter-mile section of US Highway 2, directing vehicles to slowly tread a depth of 3 inches of water until the water receeded on June 6th.

The Musselshell River at Mosby (MSBM8) rose above its flood stage of 10 feet at 11:10 PM MST on June 3rd, crested at 11.72 feet at 7:50 AM MST on June 3rd, then feel back down below flood stage at 1:10 AM MST on June 6th.

The Milk River at Dodson (DMRM8) rose above its flood stage of 23 feet at 2:30 PM MST on June 4th, crested at 25.95 feet at 4:40 PM MST on June 5th, then fell back down below flood stage at 10:45 PM MST on June 7th.

The Milk River at Tampico (TMPM8) rose above its flood stage of 23 feet at 3:40 AM MST on June 6th, crested at 24.69 feet at 5:00 AM MST on June 11th, then fell back down below flood stage at 12:15 PM MST on June 13th.

The Milk River at the Glasgow Highway 24 bridge (GLWM8) rose above its flood stage of 25 feet at 7:40 PM MST on June 4th, crested at 27.82 feet at 5:00 PM MST on June 11th, then fell back down below flood stage at 8:00 AM MST on June 18th.

Beaver Creek near the town of Hinsdale rose out of its banks on June 4th and flooded the surrounding lower-lying areas, county roads, and fields, south of US Highway 2 between the towns of Saco and Hinsdale. The tornado was first spotted about 19 miles north of Wolf Point and the NWS Storm Damage Team found downed tree limbs and a de-barked tree trunk.  As it moved eastward, the tornado rolled heavy hay bails, snapped a road-sign post and flipped a loose yard shed.  A few miles west of the Poplar River and just north of County Road 2042, the Beck Farm sustained the most damage involving roofs peeled away and blown off of several farm and storage buildings.  Winds here were estimated at 115 to 120 mph.  After crossing over the Poplar River, the tornado downed a large cottonwood tree, lifted and moved irrigation pipes, and snapped 9 power poles, then dissipated near the intersection of County Roads 2041 and 1041, about 17 miles north of Poplar.

Based on photos from emergency management and in discussion with those in the area, the wind speed is estimated to be at least 90 mph.  Trees were stripped of their leaves, windows were broken, There was a home with part of the roof torn off, windows broken a shed completely destroyed, and a nearly one hundred year old barn that had been restored in the past two years that was destroyed.

Reports from spotters, the public and emergency management indicate a very large area of significant crop loss about 5-10 miles either side of the line indicated. There are no good estimates of loss, but the few farmers we did speak to told us they lost thousands of acres, totaling in the millions of dollars of crop loss.

Ice moved into the Glendive area overnight on March 9-10.  The ice jammed in Glendive causing the water to rise over 8 feet in less than 15 minutes.  The jam caused water and ice to flow across the Marsh Road just southwest of town, and it also took out several power poles.   The ice jam further impacted the town as water and ice filled into the Toepke Park baseball/softball complex.  At least one 1,000 gallon propane tank was lifted from its base and floated down river.  The USGS gauge in Glendive peaked at 57.29 feet, but the ice caused a large area of low-land flooding downstream of the gauge for the next 36 hours.

A series of ice jams caused moderate flooding along the river in Richland County.   One farm house had water two feet over the basement window wells, and in the worst flood in 1979, it was only 2 inches over the window wells.  The ice caused rapid rises of water, and two volunteer firefighters from Savage, MT got caught as the ice came up behind them while checking the river after dark.  It took a rescue helicopter from Minot Air Force Base to come and rescue them off of the ice island they were stranded on for 5 hours.  Several propane tanks were reported to have been pulled off their stands and floated downstream.  There was a lot of farmland and low lying areas that experienced flooding all the way from the Dawson/Richland County line to the confluence with the Missouri River a few miles into North Dakota.

The initial report of flash flooding came from an NWS employee who reported that Cherry Creek on the northwest side of Glasgow has risen out of its banks and is flooding with several inches of water over Skylark Road at Martin Coulee.  The Creek was actually flooding in the area about 4 miles north of Glasgow westward and then southward to the Milk River.  Many homeowners evacuated and had to move livestock and trailers out of the flooded waters.  This is the second highest the river has been in at least 4 decades (2011 was higher).   There were over a dozen homes with water in the basements and crawl spaces, and the water was so high, many people were unable to leave their homes because the driveways were flooded over with swift moving water.

The Beaver Creek near Hinsdale (BCHM8) rose above its flood stage of 14 feet at 3:01 PM MST on August 24th, crested in major flooding at 19.52 feet at 12:30 AM MST on August 26th, then fell back down below flood stage at 6:37 AM MST on August 29th.  The crest of 19.52 feet became the new record historical crest for that gauge.

The Musselshell River at Mosby (MSBM8) rose above its flood stage of 10 feet at 7:00 PM MST on August 24th, crested in major flooding at 14.36 feet at 5:00 PM MST on August 25th, then fell back down below flood stage at 4:00 AM MST on August 27th.

The Milk River at Glasgow - Hwy 24 bridge (GLWM8) rose above its flood stage of 25 feet at 9:50 PM MST on August 24th, crested in major flooding at 31.75 feet at 12:26 AM MST on August 26th, and continued flooding into September.

Record rainfall in late August caused sustained high water and flooding at Beaver Creek near Hinsdale (BCHM8).  It rose again above its flood stage of 14 feet at 6:12 AM MST on September 3rd, crested at 14.67 feet at 6:43 PM MST on September 4th, and fell back down below flood stage at 10:30 PM MST on September 6th.

Continuing with flooding through the end of August, the Milk River at Glasgow - Highway 24 bridge (GLWM8) rose above flood stage and crested in August, then fell back down below flood stage at 11:35 AM MST on September 3rd.

Continuing with flooding through the end of August, the Milk River at Tampico (TMPM8) rose above flood stage and crested in August, then fell back down below flood stage at 12:30 AM MST on September 1st.

Damage was found at a new home site with a modular home and a large metal pole barn located 2.4 miles east of the intersection of Highway 16 and County Road 496.  There were two other home sites west of this home, with no obvious damage.  The newer home had a few missing shingles, but the new pole barn had the south door blown in with the south wall blown out to the southeast. There were a few trees that were snapped or cracked and dropped about 2-3 feet off the ground, including older Russian olive trees.  The damage to the pole barn was estimated to have been caused by 70-75 mph winds.  The homeowners were home and said the wind came from the west-northwest and there was a lot of dirt and gravel kicked up and thrown at them prior to their seeking shelter in a safe room in the pole barn.  The garage door was blown in and the south wall was blown out.  The garage door blew through the side wall and landed on a trailer near a tree row.   All the insulation and debris from the side wall collapse were blown eastward.  ||Another third of a mile east is the town site of McCabe, where there are a few homes, sheds and outbuildings.  This area had a large older Russian olive tree uprooted as well as a two healthy spruce trees uprooted that were at least 25 feet tall.  There was a shed damaged as well, but the two garage doors on it were open directly to the microburst winds, and the wood at the concrete footing was over 30 years old.  All the debris was blown eastward.  ||There was a lot of minor damage as well through the townsite.

A semi-truck was blown over due to the strong microbust winds within the squall line of thunderstorms that moved through.  Other minor damage was reported in the area as well to homes and farm outbuildings.

Over 5 to 10 inches of rainfall fell in a four day period.  This caused massive flooding in area creeks and streams.  The most significant damage was from Flatwillow Creek into the Musselshell River.  Cooperative weather observers noted it was the highest they had ever seen the water on Flatwillow Creek, including the 2011 flood season.  It was high enough that the USGS gage on Flatwillow Creek was washed out and is gone, and the Flatwillow Road bridge was also washed out.  The County DES coordinator reported over 30 locations with damages to culverts, roads and bridges with damages of at least $515,000.

Heavy rainfall in the basin with amounts ranging from 4 to 10 inches over a four day period caused significant flooding in all the streams in the basin, and eventually the rivers.  Willow Creek, Antelope Creek, Cherry Creek, Larb Creek, Brazil Creek all flooded during this time frame, blocking off many gravel roads around the county.  Valley County had at least 36 locations with damages and DES reported to FEMA the totals were $1.2 million.  Willow Creek Road from Fort Peck to the Pines had a very large area completely wiped out with a large culvert gone.

A warmer-than-normal start to the month of March allowed area creeks and drainages to freely run as the snowpack quickly melted.  As the Mid Muddy Creek flowed southward through Sheridan County, the rate of snowmelt became too much for the creek channel to handle.  It rose above the flood stage of 12 feet early in the evening of March 12th, crested at 14.09 feet on the morning of March 13th, as fell back down below flood stage later in the morning of March 12th.

A warmer-than-normal start to the month of March allowed the ice on the Poplar River to break up.  The ice breaks jammed up and began to flood the Poplar River near the town of Poplar.  The river rose above the flood stage of 15.5 feet during the afternoon of March 13th, crested at 16.35 feet later in the early morning of March 14th, and fell back down below flood stage in the early morning of March 15th.

The National Weather Service in Glasgow, along with Richland County Disaster and Emergency Services conducted a damage survey of a property.  The mobile home and its associated storage building (also a mobile home) were thrown from its foundation. The primary home lost its metal frame and was thrown onto a storage shed to the southwest, about 60 feet to the southwest. The two mobile homes, which did not appear to have been strapped down, were overturned and one had the entire frame bent and twisted. While there were tree branches broken in the region, the most significant damage was on this property site, due to the rural nature of the area.  Power poles on the property were not damaged, although the lines were snapped.  ||One 79 year old gentleman was in the home with his dog also on the property.  The gentleman was in the mobile home and suffered injuries requiring transport to a local and then regional hospital.   The dog was found trapped under rubble but was ok. ||Based off of the damage that was observed, the winds were estimated at 100 mph.     The tornado continued through rural area to the south-southeast where it went into North Dakota about 5 miles south-southeast of the property site with the damage.  No reported damage has been noted in North Dakota and the tornado dissipated south-southwest of Trotters.

The National Weather Service in Glasgow conducted a damage survey in Glendive on July 28, 2015 following a significant severe thunderstorm that hit the evening before coming in from the southwest.  NWS staff met with county and city officials before and after the survey to be briefed and brief them on what was discovered.   The event was a macroburst (large scale straight line wind event) with some microburst components in between. | 	There were not enough time and resources to enter the various neighborhoods that were impacted, and due to the number of trees and power lines down, it was not safe to try and go around these areas where crews were working.  In order to best evaluate the wind speeds, the structures with the most damage were focused on as recommended by the Emergency Operations Center staff.   Several dozen homes were viewed though, and the damage was generally due to trees and branches lost, or shingles torn off of roofs.  That includes trees in homes or on cars, some partially blown off roofs, and trailer homes or semi-trailers blown over.  The damage survey started with the power lines west-northwest of town on Highway 200, then to the Glendive airport,  Seven Mile Drive, back through town on Highway 200S, up Merrill Ave and then up Highway 16 north to Sidney for 10 miles.  |	Access to the large metal truss electrical transmission towers west-northwest of town on Highway 200S was not possible due to the extreme mud conditions.  There were at least 5 noted as having crumbled toward the ground.   Further investigation will have to be done with the owner of the structures as to the age of these towers, but at minimum the winds would���ve been 120 mph.  There are also numerous wooden poles snapped at the bases and part way up along Highway 200.   The NWS will get total numbers from utility providers once they have a chance to assess all the damage.  |At the airport, winds were gusting to 90 mph last night on an anemometer on top of the terminal roof.   The winds tore the anemometer off the roof though, so a peak wind was not measured.  The FAA AWOS station that is the official observing equipment for the airport lost power, and a maximum gust was not received from it either.    There was a large cottonwood tree that was uprooted near the terminal building.  There were three metal roof/siding airplane hangars damaged.  One was completely destroyed, and the other two had the metal roofing peeled back/off.  The one that was destroyed wasn���t cemented into the ground and the posts easily ripped out of the ground when the wind blew against it.  All the debris was blown towards the north-northeast. The winds are estimated at 90 to 95 mph at this location.  |The next stop was on Highway 200S just southeast of the Interstate turnoff.  Significant damage occurred to a large metal building.  The failure point was two large garage doors that face southwest.  There is nothing to stop the wind as it rolls through the valley towards it.  The garage doors blew in, and the roof blew off.  One of the employees mentioned that sheet metal from another building southwest of them was blown towards their building.  The impact of that metal hitting the doors may have helped cause the doors to fail and be blown in.  This metal building had solid steel I-Beams in the ceiling that were bent back where the roof peeled back.    Power poles with transformers on them were snapped off near this facility and just east-southeast of it.  The transformers are pretty heavy and the resistance and weight of them against the wind made them easy targets to be snapped. All the debris was blown in a north-northeasterly direction.  Between the building and the power poles, winds at this location are estimated to have been around 100 to 110 mph.|7 Mile Drive was next.  There were many homes with shingles peeled off, and large trees split and large branches down, metal buildings damaged and sheet metal blown around. A few power poles were also snapped.  We stopped at an office building and a newer, well-built warehouse after noticing the garage doors on the warehouse were bent out.  There was also some insulation missing on a portion of a wall.   They had already cleaned up the south side doors, which had blown in as the winds came off the hill and crumbled some of the north side doors.  There was very little noticeable roof damage, which is something you will often see with garage doors blowing in, a testament to how well the building was built and the steel I-beams used in the trusses.  Winds at this location are estimated at 100-105 mph.     |Another metal building structure was viewed south of the interstate off of 7 Mile Drive.  A large overhead door that faces south was blown in and the roof right above it peeled off and blown to the north.   On the north side of the building, the majority of the roof (with wooden trusses) was either collapsed into the building or blown north-northeastward.  Winds at this location are estimated at 95 to 100 mph.|As we went down Highway 200S into downtown, the most notable damage was tree branches down.   We went down Marsh Road, and there were a lot of trees damaged in that area from 1 to 3 miles south of town.  House damage was generally due to branches falling on them or against them.   Heading north on Merrill Ave, tree damage was the most noticed damage, specifically near the high school football field.  A large blue spruce was noted down near I-94 and roof damage with shingles and fascia torn off were noted on a new hotel at that location.  Winds in this portion of town are estimated to have been 80-90 mph.  |We continued north on Highway 16 towards Sidney.  The number of damaged trees and sheds quickly reduced as we headed north and by 10 miles we were really looking hard to see any damage.  At four miles north of town, there was a home with a new barn that had all but the west wall collapse.  With no one home, we did not go out into the field to assess the barn closer, but it was newly built.  Winds at this point are estimated at 100 mph.

Suspected human activity started a wildfire in the Little Rocky Mountains near Zortman and Landusky on the afternoon of July 3rd, and raged until the 19th with a total of 11,699 acres burned.
A grassland/wildfire was ignited on the morning of July 10th due to unknown causes. This fire burned until the morning of July 17th with a total of 3,034 acres burned.

Located in Petroleum County west of the Musselshell River and about 50 miles north of Winnett, Montana, the Crying Fire was reported mid-day July 19th and burned in grass, sage and timber on BLM, Private, State and Charles M. Russell National Wildlife Refuge lands. The fire was lightning caused. Crews responded from the U.S. Bureau of Land Management, U.S. Fish & Wildlife Service, U.S. Forest Service, Montana Department of Natural Resources and Petroleum County. No accidents or injuries occurred, although two outbuildings were lost. The fire burned 7,925 acres.

The Lodgepole Complex, which started on the afternoon of the 19th, was initially composed of 5 separate fires. The complex was located 52 miles west northwest of Jordan, Montana, and 15 miles east of Winnett, Montana. The complex burned until August 2nd and burned a total of 270,723 acres. In addition, sixteen homes were destroyed as well as an unspecified but significant amount of fencing and haystacks. Numerous secondary structures have also been destroyed. McCone Electric lost over 120 power poles. An additional 16 structures were identified via satellite imagery as destroyed but type of use has not been determined.  The Lodgepole Fire ended up being the second largest fire in Montana history.
