Despite a couple of winter storms that dropped a few inches of snow across the area the latter half of the month, precipitation amounts were generally 25 to 75 percent below normal. Extreme (D3) conditions prevailed throughout the month across Daniels County.

Despite a couple of winter storms that dropped a few inches of snow across the area the latter half of the month, precipitation amounts were generally less than 50 percent of normal for the month across the northwestern half of the county, but around normal for the southeastern half. Severe (D2) drought conditions remained in place across northwestern Dawson County.

Because of a couple of winter storms that dropped a few inches of snow across the area the latter half of the month, precipitation amounts were around normal for the month across eastern Roosevelt County. Due to the already frozen ground and this being a climatologically dry time of year, Severe (D2) drought conditions remained in place across eastern Roosevelt County.

Despite a couple of winter storms that dropped enough snow to bring precipitation amounts ranging from 75 to 200 percent of normal, Garfield County remained in Severe (D2) to Extreme (D3) drought conditions throughout December.

Despite a couple of winter storms that dropped enough snow to bring precipitation amounts to approximately 200 percent of normal, the Little Rockies remained in Severe (D2) drought conditions throughout December.

Despite a couple of winter storms that dropped enough snow to bring precipitation amounts to approximately 50 to nearly 200 percent of normal across portions of the county, McCone County remained in Severe (D2) to Extreme (D3) drought conditions throughout December.

The couple of winter storms that moved across the area were somewhat hit or miss across northern Phillips County, with precipitation amounts ranging from as low as 25 percent to as high as 200 percent of normal. Northern Phillips County remained in Extreme (D3) drought conditions throughout December.

Despite a couple of winter storms that moved across the area which produced approximately 200 percent of average precipitation for the month, northern Valley County remained in Extreme (D3) drought conditions throughout December.

Despite a couple of winter storms that moved across the area which produced approximately 150 to 200 percent of normal precipitation for the month, Petroleum County remained in Severe (D2) drought conditions throughout December.

Despite a couple of winter storms that moved across the area which produced approximately 150 to 200 percent of normal precipitation for the month, the western half of Prairie County remained in Severe (D2) drought conditions throughout December.

Despite a couple of winter storms that moved across the area which produced approximately 150 to 200 percent of normal precipitation for the month, the northwestern half of Richland County remained in Severe (D2) drought conditions throughout December.

Despite a couple of winter storms that moved across the area which produced approximately 50 percent to near normal precipitation for the month, Sheridan County remained in Severe (D2) drought conditions throughout December.

Despite a couple of winter storms that moved across the area, western Roosevelt County received only approximately 50 percent to near normal precipitation for the month, and remained in Severe (D2) drought conditions throughout December.
A trained spotter at the Buckhorn general store in Zortman reported 14 inches of snow, beginning at approximately 8:00 the morning of the 19th and ending at 2:00 PM the afternoon of the 20th.
A trained spotter located 6 miles west southwest of Chapman reported 8 to 10 inches of snow, primarily falling overnight on the 19th and into the 20th.

Even though snowfall began earlier, the main impacts from this storm were due to poor road conditions in the area. According to the MDT road conditions website, blowing and drifting snow was first reported at 10:30 AM on the 28th, and road conditions continued to be poor until around 10:00 AM on the 31st.||Although snowfall amounts of 9 to 12 inches were reported, this was spread out over the course of three days.

Snowfall reports for this storm were lacking, but enough snow fell to make roads treacherous. There were reports of snow covered roads as well as significant blowing and drifting snow throughout the area, as reported by the MDT road conditions website.

We received a 24 hour snowfall report from COOP observer 3N Brusett of 9.0 inches at 5:00 PM on the 29th. Snow was determined to be falling until 3:30 PM on the 30th, with the time the snow ended estimated based on radar observations.

Although snowfall amounts of generally less than 6 inches were reported, road conditions became very poor due to blowing and drifting snow on the morning of the 29th, and remained poor into the morning of the 31st. Road conditions were determined based on the MDT road conditions website.
Even though winds were near calm, observations at the Bluff Creek RAWS site showed temperatures less than 40 below zero on the morning of the 31st.

The Glasgow airport ASOS measured wind chills of 40 below to 55 below zero throughout the period, with a break of calm winds the evening of the 30th and into the 31st. The event continued into January 1st.
Even though winds were nearly calm, observations near the Canadian border showed consistent temperatures between 40 below and 50 below zero for this period.
The Malta AWOS measured wind chills ranging from 40 below to near 60 below during this time. Winds were generally around 10 miles per hour. The event continued into January 1st.

Temperatures were in the teens below zero much of the morning of the 1st. With easterly winds at 10 to 15 mph, wind chills were down into the 30s below zero across Garfield County, and a wind chill of 40 below was recorded at the Mesonet site near Sand Springs at 7 AM.

With temperatures in the teens below zero and winds gusting above 30 mph at times, wind chills across portions of Sheridan County were less than 40 below zero for several hours on the evening of the 1st and into the early morning hours of the 2nd.

With bitter cold temperatures dropping into the 30s below zero and easterly winds of approximately 10 mph, wind chills dropped into the 40s and even 50s below zero across western Roosevelt County, with the lowest wind chill recorded being 59 below zero at the Poplar RAWS at 8:18 AM MST.

Bitter cold temperatures and relatively light easterly winds produced wind chills of less than 50 below zero early on the morning of the 1st across portions of Valley County. The coldest wind chill recorded in the county was at the Glasgow ASOS, which recorded a wind chill of 54 degrees below zero at 3:53 AM on January 1st. This event was a continuation from the evening of December 31st, when the Glasgow ASOS recorded a wind chill of 56 degrees below zero.

With bitter cold temperatures and winds gusting to approximately 20 mph, wind chills were able to drop to less than 40 degrees below zero at a couple of locations across McCone County on the evening of the 1st. The lowest recorded wind chill was 46 degrees below zero at the Cow Creek DOT site.

Bitter cold temperatures and winds gusting to approximately 25 mph contributed to the production of extreme wind chill values of less than 40 degrees below zero over portions of Dawson County from the evening of the 1st into the early morning hours of the 2nd. The coldest wind chill recorded was 46 degrees below zero at 8:43 PM MST on the 1st.
A wind chill value of 44 degrees below zero was recorded at the Glasgow airport ASOS.
The Navajo MT-5 DOT site recorded wind chill values of less than 40 degrees below zero during this time, the coldest value being 46 below from 4:45 to 5:00 AM.
The Comertown Turn-Off MT-5 DOT site recorded wind chills of less than 40 degrees below zero during this time, with a minimum of 46 below from 6:30 to 7:45 AM.
The mesonet site in Scobey recorded wind chills of less than 40 degrees below zero during this time, with a minimum of 44 below zero at 7:30 AM.
The Sioux Pass MT-16 DOT site recorded wind chills of less than 40 degrees during this time, the coldest being 43 below zero at 7:30 AM.
The US-2 @Stateline DOT site recorded wind chill values of 40 degrees below zero or less during this time, with a minimum value of 41 below at 9 AM.

Temperatures across much of Valley County dropped into the teens below zero with winds gusting to 15 to 20 mph. This was enough to create widespread wind chill values of less than 30 below zero, with a couple of spots seeing wind chills at 40 below or less, mainly at the Glasgow airport ASOS.

Temperatures across much of Roosevelt County dropped into the teens below zero with winds gusting to 15 to 20 mph. This was enough to create widespread wind chill values of less than 30 below zero, with the Poplar RAWS site recording a wind chill of 41 below.

Widespread wind chills in the 30s below zero occurred in Daniels County the evening of the 26th and the early morning of the 27th, with the Navajo MT-5 DOT site periodically recording wind chills less than 40 below.

Reports on the KLTZ radio station's social media page indicated that several people in the town of St Marie could not get out of their driveways due to blowing and drifting snow, and that even an ambulance had to call for a snow plow to get in and out of town. New snowfall amounts ranged from approximately 2 to 5 inches. Time is estimated.

Montana DOT road condition reports showed snow covered roads as well as blowing and drifting and blowing snow. Highway 200 was snow covered as early as 7:00 AM, and blowing and drifting snow was observed into the afternoon. Approximately 4 to 5 inches of new snowfall was reported.

Montana Department of Transportation road condition maps showed snow covered roads as well as blowing and drifting snow, starting at around 5:30 AM. Although this continued well into the night, by the evening winds had diminished enough to be below warning criteria. Snowfall amounts of approximately 3 inches were reported.

Montana Department of Transportation road condition maps showed snow covered roads as well as blowing and drifting snow, starting at around 5:30 AM. Although this continued well into the night, by the evening winds had diminished enough to be below warning criteria. Two to three inches of new snowfall was reported.

Montana Department of Highways road conditions maps showed significant blowing and drifting snow across roads in Wibaux County. This began around 9:30 AM and persisted into the evening. Snowfall amounts of approximately 3 inches were reported.
Snow and significant blowing snow was reported across roads and highways in the area, starting about 1 PM and lasting into the evening.

Snow and significant blowing snow was reported across roads and highways in the area, starting about 1 PM and lasting into the evening. New snowfall totals were approximately 2 to 4 inches across the county.

The combination of light to moderate snowfall and gusty winds created visibility and road conditions issues due to blowing and drifting snow on the afternoon of the 10th. The area received generally between 3 and 5 inches of snow from this storm.

Bitter cold temperatures and winds gusting to approximately 25 mph contributed to the production of wind chill values of less than 30 degrees below zero over portions of Prairie County on the 1st, and once dropped values to less than 40 below. The coldest wind chill recorded was 48 degrees below zero at 4:08 AM MST on the 1st, recorded at the Big Sheep Mountain RAWS.

Archived Montana Department of Transportation road reports showed poor road conditions with blowing and drifting snow beginning at around 6:00 AM MST on the 10th. Roads continued to be snow covered until around 9:00 AM MST on the 11th. Additionally, a trained spotter located 4 miles east-northeast of Flatwillow reported 8 inches of snowfall that lasted from the evening of the 9th until approximately 1:00 PM MST on the 10th.

Wind chills at both the Poplar RAWS and the Comertown Montana Department of Transportation sites dropped to less than 40 below zero from approximately 8:15 AM MST on the 12th, remaining below or near 40 below zero until approximately 7:15 AM MST on the 13th. Winds were generally from the south, then shifted to the northeast at approximately 10 miles per hour.

Winds at the Montana DOT site 35 miles south of Malta gusted to 58 miles per hour or greater between 7:11 AM MST and 7:30 AM MST on the morning of the 30th. The peak gust was 61 miles per hour at 7:11 AM MST.

The month of January began with northern Phillips county experiencing severe (D2) drought conditions. Even though the area received a few inches of snow during the month, there was no appreciable recovery in the drought by the beginning of February.

The month of January began with central and southeast Phillips county experiencing severe (D2) drought conditions. Even though a couple of locations received 4 to 6 inches of snow during the month, there was no significant recovery in the drought by the beginning of February.

The month of January began with northern Valley county experiencing severe (D2) drought conditions. Even though the area received a few inches of snow during the month, there was no significant recovery in the drought by the beginning of February.

The month of January began with central and southern Valley county experiencing severe (D2) drought conditions. Even though the area received a few inches of snow during the month, there was no significant recovery in the drought by the beginning of February.

The month of January began with Daniels County experiencing severe (D2) drought conditions. Only one to two inches of snow fell during the month, and there was no significant recovery in the drought by the beginning of February.

The month of January began with Sheridan County experiencing severe (D2) drought conditions. Only one to three inches of snow fell during the month, and there was no appreciable recovery in the drought by the beginning of February.

The month of January began with western Roosevelt County experiencing severe (D2) drought conditions. Very little snow fell during the month across most of the area, and there was no appreciable recovery in the drought by the beginning of February.

The month of January began with eastern Roosevelt County experiencing severe (D2) drought conditions. Only one to two inches of snow fell during the month across most of the area, and there was no appreciable recovery in the drought by the beginning of February.

The month of January began with the northern and central portions of Garfield County experiencing severe (D2) drought conditions. Even though a few inches of snow fell during the month across the area, there was no appreciable recovery in the severe drought conditions by the beginning of February.

The month of January began with the northern portions of McCone County experiencing severe (D2) drought conditions. Even though a few inches of snow fell during the month across the area, there was no appreciable recovery in the severe drought conditions by the beginning of February.
The Petroleum County sheriff reported 8 inches of new snow with drifts up to approximately two to three feet deep. Light snow was still falling at 8 AM on the 5th but stopped shortly after.

Road conditions were treacherous due to drifting and blowing snow. At around 1 AM local time, Highway 200 was closed east of Winnett due to severe driving conditions and a semi trailer blocking the road. The Montana DOT road conditions web-site showed improving conditions by 7 AM.
Cooperative observers east northeast of Flatwillow and north northeast of Winnett reported 24 hour snowfall totals of six to eight inches.

Observations from multiple sources, including Montana Department of Transportation sites and cooperative observers, showed that generally 4 to 10 inches of snow fell across central and southeast Phillips County from the late evening on the 7th through the day on the 8th. The greatest snowfall reported was 10 inches at a Department of Transportation site south of Malta. Road conditions were treacherous on the 8th, with ice and snow covered roads as well as reduced visibility due to blowing and drifting snow.

Across central and southern Valley county, 3 to 6 inches of new snowfall were common.  Up to 8 inches of snow was reported approximately 45 miles southwest of Glasgow. Road conditions were treacherous on the 8th, with ice and snow covered roads as well as reduced visibility due to blowing and drifting snow.
Up to 9 inches of snow fell across the area from the night of the 7th and through the day on the 8th. Roads across the area, including Highway 200, were ice and snow covered with significant drifts.

Generally 5 to 9 inches of snow fell across Garfield County from the night of the 7th and through the day on the 8th. There were reports of 9 inches from a cooperative observer 4 miles east northeast of Mosby and 12 inches from a cooperative observer 3 miles north of Brusett. Roads across the area, including Highway 200, were ice and snow covered with significant drifts.

Several inches of snow fell across Prairie County the night of the 7th through the morning hours on the 9th. Cooperative observers reported 5 inches of snow in 24 hours 5 miles north of Mildred, and 8 inches in Terry. The 8 inch storm total was 4 inches in two 24 hour periods. Additionally, roads became snow and ice covered, leading to treacherous driving conditions.
Northern Phillips County received 3 to 5 inches of snow from this storm system. Blowing and drifting snow created treacherous driving conditions throughout the day on the 8th.

Several inches of snow fell across the area from the night of the 7th and throughout the day on the 8th. Roads across the area, including Highway 191, were ice and snow covered with significant drifts. A cooperative observer in Zortman reported a 2 day snowfall total of 10 inches.

Wind chills at the Poplar AWOS dropped under 40 below at approximately 10:15 PM on the 9th, and stayed near or below that point until approximately 6:30 on the morning of the 10th. The McDonalds Montana Department of Transportation site recorded wind chills under 40 below from approximately midnight on the morning of the 10th to 4:30 on the morning of the 10th.

Temperatures across Garfield County dropped into the 20s and 30s below zero on the night of the 9th and the early morning of the 10th. Even with winds ranging from calm to 10 miles per hour, wind chills periodically dropped to 40 below zero or less between just before midnight on the 9th and approximately 4:00 on the morning of the 10th.

Temperatures in the 20s below zero and fairly light winds combined to produce bitterly cold wind chills across the area. A 40 below zero wind chill value was recorded by the Glasgow airport ASOS at 8:53 PM on the evening of the 9th.
Temperatures in the teens and 20s below and relatively light winds combined to produce bitterly cold wind chill values at Glendive early in the morning of the 10th.
A wind chill value of 40 below zero was recorded at the Sioux Pass Montana Department of Transportation site.

Temperatures at the Malta Airport were less than 20 below zero with winds of approximately 10 mph, which contributed to extreme wind chill values of less than 40 below zero from 11:15 AM to 2:15 PM on the 12th. The coldest wind chill value was 47 below zero, which occurred at 11:15 AM.
The Saco US-2 DOT site recorded extreme wind chills of less than 40 below zero from 8:46 PM to 9:36 PM the evening of the 12th, and again from 2:07 to 2:27 AM the morning of the 13th.
The mesonet site at the Whitewater school recorded a wind chill value of 40 below zero at 2:15 AM the morning of the 13th.

Observations at the Malta Airport AWOS site showed wind chill values less than 40 below zero from 6:35 PM the evening of the 9th through 11:55 AM the morning of the 10th. The lowest wind chill value was 58 below zero, occurring from 5:15 AM through 8:15 AM the morning of the 10th.
The Montana Department of Transportation site recorded a wind chill value of 41 below zero at 6:38 AM on the 10th.
The mesonet site at the Whitewater school recorded a wind chill value of 60 below zero at 5:10 AM on the 12th.

The drought from 2017 continued through the month of February across northern Valley County. Even with 8 to 10 inches of snow across the area during the month, which was two hundred to three hundred percent of the normal amount, drought recovery has been slow. Severe (D2) drought conditions persisted throughout the month.

Severe (D2) drought conditions persisted across central and southern Valley County throughout the month, but some improvement was observed. Western portions of this zone did improve to Moderate (D1) drought conditions in February, helped in large part by the one to over three feet of snow that fell during the month. A few locations, including areas from near Glasgow and to the southwest, received over 600 percent of the normal precipitation.

Northern Phillips started February experiencing Severe (D2) drought conditions, but showed significant improvement by February 13th, improving to Moderate (D1) drought conditions. This was due in large part to a significant winter storm that produced four to six inches of snow on February 7th and 8th. Total snowfall for the entire month averaged approximately eight to twelve inches. Snowfall for the month was two hundred to four hundred percent of normal.

Central and southeast Phillips started February experiencing Severe (D2) drought conditions, but showed significant improvement by February 13th, improving to Moderate (D1) drought conditions. This was due in large part to a significant winter storm that produced eight to twelve inches of snow on February 7th and 8th. There was further improvement to Abnormally Dry (D0) conditions by the end of the month due to additional snowfall. Total snowfall for the entire month averaged approximately one to three feet.

Daniels County experienced Severe (D2) drought conditions throughout the month of February. The far northeast corner of the area was the driest by far, with Daniels County receiving only about two to four inches of snow. This was still one hundred to two hundred percent of normal, but the precipitation amounts were not enough to affect the drought.

Sheridan County experienced Severe (D2) drought conditions throughout the month of February. The far northeast corner of the area was the driest by far, with Sheridan County receiving only about one to four inches of snow, which was fifty percent of normal to just above normal.

Western Roosevelt County experienced Severe (D2) drought conditions throughout the month of February. Even with five to seven inches of snow throughout February, which was two hundred to four hundred percent of normal, drought conditions persisted across western Roosevelt County.

Eastern Roosevelt County experienced Severe (D2) drought conditions throughout the month of February. With four to six inches of snow throughout February, which was approximately 75 to 90 percent of normal, drought conditions persisted across eastern Roosevelt County.

Central and northern Garfield entered February experiencing Severe (D2) drought conditions. The area experienced improvement to Moderate (D1) drought conditions due to significant snowfall over the first half of the month. There was further improvement to Abnormally Dry (D0) drought conditions due to more snowfall over the latter half of the month. Snowfall amounts averaged 20 to 30 inches across much of Garfield County during February, which was 400 to over 600 percent of normal.

The northern section of McCone County experienced Severe (D2) drought conditions throughout the month of February. Even with approximately 300 percent of normal precipitation, the three to six inches of snowfall were not enough to make a significant impact on the drought during February.
An NWS employee traveling in the area reported very slick conditions, with at least a quarter of an inch of freezing rain, covered by 3 to 4 inches of snow.
A 60 mph peak wind gust was measured at the Glendive Airport AWOS.

Flash flooding was reported by Prairie County DES personnel on Old Highway 10, or about 6 miles east of Terry. This was due to thunderstorms over the area that produced over an inch and a half of rain in less than an hour. The Mesonet site TWSM8 1 mile southeast of Terry, recorded 1.68 inches of rain from these thunderstorms.
A 76 mph thunderstorm wind gust was measured by an automated weather station.

Several inches of snow fell across central and southern Phillips County with this storm. Widespread snowfall amounts were 4 to 7 inches, with up to 12 inches reported at the Montana Department of Transportation site south of Malta on Highway 191. Montana road reports showed snow and blowing snow significantly impacting travel conditions as early as noon on the 4th. Highway 191 was closed due to the severe travel conditions from approximately 8:00 on the evening of March 4th and did not reopen until the early morning hours of March 6th.

Montana road reports show blowing and drifting snow significantly impacting travel as early as noon on the 4th of March. By 8 AM on the 5th, there were multiple reports from the Zortman area of 12 to 15 inches of new snowfall with drifts over 4 feet deep.
Heavy snow fell across Valley County with this storm. Widespread snowfall amounts were over 6 inches, with the highest being 15 inches, which was measured at the Glasgow Weather Forecast Office.

Several inches of snow fell across northern Valley County with this storm. Snowfall amounts of up to 14 inches were reported with this storm, with 10 inches falling on the 4th alone at a cooperative observation site north of Opheim.

Very sparse snowfall reports came in from Daniels County for this storm. However, Montana DOT road reports showed severe driving conditions across Daniels County due to blowing and drifting snow beginning at 8:30 PM on the 4th, and lasting into the evening of the 5th.

Snow began falling in Sheridan County at around 7 AM on March 4th. Snowfall diminished overnight on the 4th, but returned with gusty winds the morning of the 5th. By 6:30 AM, blowing and drifting snow had reduced visibility to blizzard conditions, and these conditions persisted until around 6 PM on the 5th. Snow stopped falling at around 11 PM on the 5th. Four to six inches of snowfall was reported across Sheridan County from this storm.

Snow began falling early in the morning of March 4th. Gusty winds accompanying the snow on the 5th created blizzard conditions as visibility was consistently reduced to less than a quarter mile across the area from approximately 11:30 AM to 2:30 PM on the 5th, as recorded on the Wolf Point ASOS and the Poplar AWOS. Three to six inches of snow fell across western Roosevelt County from this storm. Snowfall diminished and ended on the evening of the 5th.

Eight to twelve inches of snow were reported across Petroleum County, most of which fell on March 4th. Eight inches of snow was reported by a cooperative observer 6 miles NNE  of Winnett at 10PM on March 4th, and a trained spotter reported a storm total of 12 inches of snow in Winnett at 9 AM on March 5th.

Heavy snow fell across portions of Garfield County the evening of March 4th through much of March 5th. At 8:30 AM MST on the 5th, a trained spotter located 7 miles southwest of the Hell Creek Recreation Area reported an estimated 12 inches of snow with drifts six to seven feet deep and reduced visibility due to wind gusts of 35 to 45 mph. Additionally, at 5 PM MST on the 5th a cooperative observer 3 miles north of Brusett reported a 24 hour snowfall total of 12 inches.

Snowfall reports were very sparse across McCone County, but reports show that over 4 inches of snow fell across the area on March 4th and 5th. Blowing and drifting snow caused significantly reduced visibility and severe travel conditions, especially after 9:00 PM MST March 4th through most of the day on the 5th.

Five to six inches of snow fell across Richland County on the 4th and 5th of the month. Gusty winds and the new snowfall created blizzard conditions from 6:45 AM MST on the 5th until just after 1:00 PM MST on the 5th.

Few snowfall reports were received from northern Phillips County. However, gusty winds, a much above normal snowpack, and fresh snow contributed to create severe driving conditions due to reduced visibility from blowing and drifting of snow across roadways. These conditions prevailed from the afternoon of March 4th through the morning of the 5th.

Three to six inches of snow fell across Wibaux County from this storm, almost entirely between just after midnight on the morning of March 5th and 3:30 PM MST on the 5th. Of greater impact, however, were gusty winds contributing to blowing and drifting snow across roadways as early as 7:00 AM MST on March 4th. Blizzard conditions were observed much of the morning and early afternoon of the 5th, with visibility down to 50 yards or less during some of this time.

Snowfall reports were difficult to come by, with 4 to 6 inches of snow being reported across Dawson County. However, the snow and gusty winds created hazardous travel conditions due to snow blowing and drifting across roadways. Blizzard conditions were observed at Glendive through much of the early morning hours of March 5th. This was concurrent with winds gusting to 50 mph or greater. The hazardous travel conditions across Dawson County persisted from the early morning hours of March 4th through the morning hours of the 5th.

Snowfall amounts across eastern Roosevelt County were generally in the 6 to 10 inch range, with the cooperative observer in Culbertson reporting 8 inches of new snow on March 4th and 5th, with an additional 4 inches in the 24 hour period between 6 PM MST March 5-6. Additionally, gusty winds contributed to blowing and drifting snow across roadways throughout this period.

Blizzard conditions with visibility of a quarter mile or less due to blowing snow were observed by the Sidney airport AWOS. Wind gusts were 35 to 45 mph during this time. Additionally, by late morning the Richland County's Sheriff's office was advising emergency travel only due to blizzard conditions impacting travel.

A cooperative observer located 9 miles northwest of Carlyle reported snow and blowing snow starting at around midnight. The majority of the snow fell after 10 AM on the 5th, and by about 8:45 PM, they reported visibility down to 50 yards due to the blowing snow.

Snow and blowing snow impacted Dawson County, causing blizzard conditions through much of the 5th. The Glendive AWOS recorded sustained winds of 35 mph or greater starting at 5:30 AM and persisting into the early afternoon hours. This caused significantly reduced visibility, and visibility was below or near a quarter mile until shortly after 5 PM on the 5th.

Snow and blowing snow reduced visibility significantly to around a quarter of a mile by 8:45 on the morning of the 23rd, as observed by the mesonet site at Plentywood. Visibility was reduced to a quarter of a mile through the rest of the morning, but significant travel impacts were reported throughout the afternoon.

During the evening of March 12st, at the Mosby river forecast point (MSBM8) along the Musselshell River, an ice jam suddenly caused the river level to briefly rise above the flood stage of 10 feet at 5:24 PM MST. Even though the river fell back down below 10 feet just 9 minutes later, at 5:33 PM MST, it quickly rose above 10 feet again at 6:14 PM MST. The river crested at 11.53 feet at 6:59 PM MST. As the ice jam cleared, the river fell back down below flood stage at 7:20 PM MST.

Northern Valley County entered March experiencing Severe (D2) drought conditions. By March 20th, conditions had improved to Moderate (D1) drought conditions. This was due to the two to three inches of liquid equivalent precipitation that fell during the month, which was approximately twice the normal amount for the area. This occurred primarily during the first week of the month, during which a foot or more of snow fell.

Central and southern Valley County entered March experiencing Severe (D2) drought conditions. By March 20th, conditions had improved to Moderate (D1) drought conditions. This was due to the two to three inches of liquid equivalent precipitation that fell during the month, which was approximately twice the normal amount for the area. This occurred primarily during the first week of the month, during which a foot or more of snow fell.

Daniels County entered March experiencing Severe (D2) drought conditions, which persisted through the month. The area received generally one and a half to two inches of liquid equivalent precipitation, which was a little below normal for the area.

Daniels County entered March experiencing Severe (D2) drought conditions, which persisted through the month. The area received generally one and a half to two inches of liquid equivalent precipitation, which was up to twice the normal amount in some cases. Even so, this was a very dry winter across Sheridan County, so this did not provide enough moisture to make a significant impact on the drought during the month of March.

Western Roosevelt County entered March experiencing Severe (D2) drought conditions, which persisted through the month, although improvement was seen by April 3rd. The area received generally one to two inches of liquid equivalent precipitation, which was up to twice the normal amount.

Eastern Roosevelt County entered March experiencing Severe (D2) drought conditions, which persisted through the month, although improvement was seen by April 3rd. The area received generally one to one and a half inches of liquid equivalent precipitation, which was up to twice the normal amount.

During the evening of March 23rd, at the Glendive river forecast point (GNDM8) along the Yellowstone River, an ice jam suddenly caused the river level to briefly rise above the flood stage of 53.5 feet at 7:45 PM MST. The river crested at 59.07 feet at 8:30 PM MST. As the ice jam cleared, the river fell back down below flood stage at 10:15 PM MST.

The Montana Department of Highways archived road reports show that significant blowing and drifting snow created hazardous driving conditions across Sheridan County during the afternoon and early evening hours of March 30th.

Severe (D2) drought conditions were experienced across eastern Daniels County throughout the month of April. The drought was relieved by one to three inches of liquid water equivalent in the area, which was more than twice the normal amount of precipitation for April. Conditions were shown to have improved by the Drought Monitor on May 1st.

Severe (D2) drought conditions were experienced across much of Sheridan County throughout the month of April. The drought was relieved by half an inch to one and a half inches of liquid water equivalent in the area, which was up to 150 percent of the normal amount of precipitation for April. Conditions were shown to have improved by the Drought Monitor to Moderate (D1) drought conditions April 17th for the eastern two thirds of the county, and on May 1st for the western third of the county.

This storm began with rain on the evening of April 1st. As temperatures dropped overnight, the precipitation transitioned to snow, and the Montana Department of Transportation observed roads were snow covered and icy. Additionally, winds gusting to 25 to 30 mph were causing travel difficulties across Petroleum County. These conditions persisted into the evening of April 2nd. Snowfall totals from cooperative observers in this storm ranged from 4 inches at Winnett 12 SW to 8 inches at Flatwillow 4 ENE.

This storm began with rain on the evening of April 1st. As temperatures dropped overnight, the precipitation transitioned to snow, and the Montana Department of Transportation observed roads were snow covered and icy by the morning of the 2nd. Additionally, winds gusting to 25 to 30 mph were causing travel difficulties across the Little Rockies and southwestern Phillips County. These conditions persisted into the evening of April 2nd. Snowfall totals from this storm ranged from 2 to 4 inches.

Snow began falling across southwest Garfield County at approximately 9 PM MST on the night of April 1st. By around 11 AM MST on the 2nd, 4 to 6 inches of snow had fallen across much of Garfield County. Additionally, blowing and drifting snow were causing travel difficulties, especially along Highway 200. The storm slowly moved out of the area late on the 2nd.

The winter storm had the greatest impact on Petroleum County, with cooperative observers reporting 8 to 10 inches of snow across the area, the majority of which fell from shortly during the morning of April 13th.

Rainfall amounts from the previous few months were around one half to one inch below normal across the northern edge and northeastern corner of northern Phillips County. After the first week of August, as the vegetation dried out, drought conditions (D2 - Severe) began there by August 7th. The latter part of the month provided some relief with one to two inches of precipitation, which was just below normal for August across the most heavily impacted areas. As recovery was still far away, drought conditions persisted into September.

During the evening of March 21st, at the Glendive forecast point (GNDM8) along the Yellowstone River, an ice jam caused the river level to briefly rise above the flood stage of 53.5 feet at 10:12 PM MST. The river crested at 54.96 feet at 10:56 AM MST on the 22nd. As the ice jam quickly cleared, the river suddenly fell back down below flood stage at 11:55 AM MST on the 22nd.

During the afternoon of March 21st, at the Hinsdale forecast point (BCHM8) along Beaver Creek, recent snow melt and an ice jam caused the river level to suddenly rise above the flood stage of 14.0 feet at 4:47 PM MST. The creek crested at 17.15 feet at 12:12 AM MST on the 23rd. As the ice jam gradually cleared, the creek fell back down below flood stage temporarily during the afternoon of the 24th, then rose again above flood stage near mid day on the 25th. The creek finally fell below flood stage to end this flood event at 10:13 AM MST on the 27th.

McCone County Sheriff's Office reported that some area back roads are impassible due to recent snow melt causing rising creek levels along the smaller tributaries feeding into the Redwater River. Most impacts were along and near the Brockway East Road and and the Dry Ash Creek Road due to culverts washing out along the Tusler Creek.  Flood start and end times are estimated.

Richland County DES Coordinator reported the Yellowstone River out of its banks and flooding low lying areas east and south of Highway 200 due to an ice jam just east of Fairview.  Flood start and end times estimated.

During the morning of March 22nd, at the Poplar forecast point (PLRM8) along the Poplar River, recent snow melt and possible ice jams caused the river level to rise above the flood stage of 13.0 feet at 9:39 AM MST.  The river crested at 20.61 feet at 1:43 PM MST on the 25th. The river level remained high and flooding continued through the end of the month.

During the morning of March 24th, at the Sidney forecast point (SIDM8) along the Yellowstone River, an ice jam caused the river level to briefly rise above the flood stage of 19.0 feet at 7:52 AM MST. The river crested at 19.59 feet at 1:27 PM MST on the 24th. As the ice jam cleared, the river fell back down below flood stage at 4:55 PM MST on the 24th.

During the afternoon of March 29th, at the Wolf Point river forecast point (WPTM8) along the Missouri River, an ice jam caused the river level to briefly rise above the flood stage of 23.0 feet at 4:12 PM MST. The river crested at 23.71 feet at 4:44 PM MST on the 29th. As the ice jam cleared, the river temporarily fell back down below flood stage for just a few minutes before rising above flood stage again. Finally, the river fell below flood stage to end this event at 7:20 PM MST on the 29th.

During the early morning of March 23rd, at the Saco forecast point (SACM8) along the Milk River, recent snow melt and a possible ice jams caused the river level to quickly rise above the flood stage of 20.0 feet at 4:35 AM MST. Between multiple ice jams, the river level dropped back down below flood stage for just a few hours the next day before rising above flood stage again.  The river crested at 21.97 feet at 1:54 PM MST on the 25th. As the ice jam gradually cleared, the river fell back down below flood stage at 11:00 PM MST on the 27th.

Excessive snow melt caused flooding at the river gauge on Beaver Creek near Hinsdale (BCHM8) two separate times through the first week of March. First, the gauge recorded creek levels rising above flood stage of 14.0 feet at 9:49 PM MST on March 1st. The creek crested at 15.8 feet at 3:28 PM MST on March 2nd. The creek level dropped back down below flood stage at 6:49 PM MST on March 3rd.  Second, the gauge recorded creek levels rising again above flood stage of 14.0 feet at 10:29 PM MST on March 5th.  The creek crested at 14.04 feet at 11:58 PM MST on March 5th, then crested again at 14.04 feet at 2:00 AM MST on March 6th.  The creek level finally dropped back down below flood stage to end this event at 4:15 AM MST on March 6th.

Excessive snow melt caused flooding at the river gauge on the Milk River near Glasgow (GLWM8). The gauge recorded river levels rising above the flood stage of 25.0 feet at 10:59 AM MST on March 6th. The Milk River at Tampico gauge (TMPM8) had been transmitting erroneous data for the previous week or so due to issues with the gage. With the flood stage set at 23.0 feet, the gauge immediately showed the river at 23.4 feet at 4:13 PM MST.  Through the rest of the day to end the month of March, the river had risen to a level of 23.5 feet. This flooding continued into the first few days of April.

Continuing from the end of March, the Milk River at Tampico (TMPM8), with a flood stage at 23.0 feet, began the first day of April at 23.5 feet. The river crested at 23.6 feet on April 1st from 7:29 AM MST to 9:45 AM MST, then fell back down below flood stage on April 2nd at 2:56 AM MST.

For central and western portions of Garfield County, sustained winds of at least 40 mph and the first severe wind gust of 61 mph were first recorded at the Lufborough Hill DOT site (MTLUF) at 4:07 PM MST.  The peak wind gust of 74 mph was also recorded there at 4:20 PM MST.  The final severe wind gust of 71 mph was recorded at Jordan airport ASOS site (KJDN) at 4:32 PM MST.

At the Malta South US-191 DOT site (MTMAL), sustained winds near or greater than 40 mph were common for about 1 1/2 hours the the late morning, then for about 30 minutes during the mid afternoon.  The peak wind gust of 62 mph was recorded at 3:09 PM MST and the final severe wind gust of 60 mph was recorded at 3:15 PM MST.

Sustained winds of 40 mph and severe wind gusts of 58 mph began at the Lindsay Divide MT-200 DOT site (MTLND) at 5:38 PM MST, then arrived at the Beaver Hill I-94 DOT site (MTBVR) around 6:30 PM MST.  The peak wind gust of 62 mph was recorded at the Beaver Hill I-94 DOT site from 6:38 PM to 6:44 PM MST.
At the Sidney airport ASOS site (KSDY), visibility of a quarter mile or less was recorded for about 1 1/2 hours in the evening on the 8th.
At the Culbertson airport mesonet site, visibility of a quarter mile or less was intermittent - for 2 1/4 hours on the night of the 8th, then again for 1 hour in the early morning on the 9th.
At multiple locations near the Missouri River valley of western Roosevelt County, visibility of a quarter mile or less was recorded from the night of the 8th through the early morning of the 9th.
At the Glasgow airport ASOS site (KGGW), visibility of a quarter mile or less was recorded intermittently through the early and mid-morning hours on the 9th.

At the Malta airport AWOS site (KM75), visibility of a quarter mile or less was recorded for about 8 hours from the afternoon of the 8th into the early morning of the 9th, then again for 2 hours on the morning of the 10th.

In the area surrounding and including the Little Rocky Mountains of southwestern Phillips County, sudden severe wind gusts began at 11:21 AM MST on the 13th, and persisted at least each hour through all the rest of that day and through 1:00 AM MST on the 14th. At the Malta South US-191 DOT site (MTMAL), the peak wind gust of 73 mph was recorded both around 2:00 PM MST and 8:30 PM MST on the 13th.  After winds subsided somewhat through the morning of the 14th, sustained winds of at least 40 mph returned for more than 3 hours during the afternoon of the 14th.

Across multiple locations in central and southeast Phillips County, sustained winds of at least 40 mph and wind gusts of at least 58 mph were recorded for about 2 1/2 hours in the early afternoon of the 13th.  The peak wind gust of 71 mph was measured at the Saco US-2 DOT site (MTSCO) around 2:30 PM MST on the 13th.

At the Bluff Creek RAWS site (BLUM8), strong sustained winds and severe wind gusts were common for most of the afternoon and evening on the 13th.  The peak wind gust of 71 mph was recorded at 4:44 PM MST.

At multiple locations across central and southern Valley County, sustained winds of at least 40 mph and/or wind gusts of at least 58 mph began as early as 1:35 PM MST on the 13th, and ended as late as 3:20 PM MST on the 14th, with some hours of weaker winds interspersed overnight.  The peak wind gust of 79 mph was recorded at the Glasgow airport ASOS site (KGGW) at 9:05 PM MST on the 13th.

At multiple sites across McCone County, sustained winds of at least 40 mph and wind gusts of at least 58 mph lasted at least intermittently from the afternoon of the 13th to the afternoon of the 14th. The peak wind gust of 71 mph was recorded at the Fort Peck Dam handar mesonet site at 10:50 PM MST on the 13th.

Sustained winds of at least 40 mph and/or wind gusts of at least 58 mph began as early at 11:41 AM MST and lasted through 5:52 PM MST on the 13th across Petroleum County.  The peak wind gust of 72 mph was recorded at 2:41 PM MST on the 13th at the Dry Blood Creek RAWS site (DBCM8).

From multiple locations across Garfield county, sustained winds of at least 40 mph and/or wind gusts of at least 58 mph began as early as 12:08 MST on the 13th.  After intermittently pausing and returning over the following day or so, it ended as late as 3:43 PM MST on the 14th.  The peak wind gust of 88 mph was recorded at 2:08 PM MST on the 13th at the South Sawmill Creek RAWS site (SSMM8).

Across central and eastern Daniels County, sustained winds of at least 40 mph and/or wind gusts of at least 58 mph began as early as 1:43 PM MST on the 13th and lasted as long a 2:41 PM MST on the 14th.  The peak wind gust of 75 mph was recorded from 11:26 PM to 11:31 PM MST on the night of the 13th at the Navajo MT-5 DOT site (MTRED).

Sustained winds of at least 40 mph and wind gusts in excess of 58 mph were common across multiple Sheridan County locations from the afternoon of the 13th into the afternoon of the 14th.  The peak wind gust of 85 mph was recorded at 11:11 PM MST on the 13th at the Comertown Turn-Off MT-5 DOT site (MTCOM).

For multiple locations across eastern Roosevelt County sustained winds of at least 40 mph and wind gusts of at least 58 mph occurred mainly from the evening through the late night of the 13th, but lingered intermittently through the morning of the 14th as well.  The peak wind gust of 68 mph was recorded at the US-2 @Stateline DOT site (MTSTA).

Sustained winds of at least 40 mph and/or wind gusts of at least 58 mph occurred at least steadily each hour from the afternoon of the 13th, to a bit less regularly through the afternoon of the 14th.  The peak wind gust of 74 mph was measured from 11:16 PM to 11:19 PM MST on the 13th at the McDonalds MT-13 DOT site (MTMCD).

For multiple locations across Richland County, sustained winds of at least 40 mph and/or wind gusts of at least 58 mph were common at least from the afternoon of the 13th into the overnight hours early on the 14th.  The peak wind gusts of 61 mph were recorded both at 7:01 PM MST on the 13th at the Badger Creek mesonet site (F2498), and from 11:53 PM MST on the 13th to 12:13 AM MST on the 14th at the Sioux Pass MT-16 DOT site (MTSOO).

Intermittent, multiple-hour periods of sustained winds of at least 40 mph and/or wind gusts of at least 58 mph were recorded from the afternoon of the 13th to the afternoon of the 14th.  The peak wind gusts of 70 mph were measured at the Lindsay Divide MT-200 DOT site (MTLND) from 11:18 PM to 11:23 PM MST on the 13th.

From the afternoon of the 13th to the afternoon of the 14th, intermittent, multiple-hour periods of sustained winds of at least 40 mph and/or wind gusts of at least 58 mph were measured across Prairie County.  The peak wind gust of 71 mph was recorded at 12:08 AM MST on the 14th at the Big Sheep Mountain RAWS site (LCFM8).

From the afternoon of the 13th through the entire day and night of the 14th, a nearly continuous period of sustained winds in excess of 40 mph and wind gusts well in excess of 58 mph were recorded in western Wibaux County.  The peak wind gusts of 81 mph were measured from 12:17 AM to 12:23 AM MST on the 14th at the Beaver Hill I-94 DOT site (MTBVR).

Wind gusts of at least 58 mph began during the night of the 19th, and intermittently lasted through the overnight hours into the 20th.  The peak wind gust of 67 mph was recorded at the Zortman RAWS site (ALDM8) at 12:32 AM MST.
At the Malta airport AWOS site (KM75), visibility dropped to a quarter mile or less from the evening of the 30th into the midnight hour on the 31st.
At the Glendive airport ASOS site (KGDV), visibility dropped to a quarter mile or less from the late night of the 30th into the early morning of the 31st.
At the Sidney airport ASOS site (KSDY), visibility dropped to a quarter mile or less from the early morning through the mid-morning on the 31st.

For multiple sites across Sheridan County, temperatures in the teens and 20s below zero and breezy winds created wind chills of -40 or worse beginning as early as the night of the 5th and lasting as long as the early morning of the 14th. For multiple sites across western Roosevelt County, temperatures in the teens and 20s below zero and breezy winds created wind chills of -40 or worse beginning as early as the early morning of the 6th and lasting as long as the early morning of the 14th. For multiple sites across McCone County, although initially in a more isolated way,  temperatures below -20 and breezy winds created wind chills of at least -40 or worse beginning as early as the morning of the 6th and lasting as late as the morning of the 14th. For multiple sites across Dawson County, although initially in a more isolated way, temperatures below -20 and breezy winds created wind chills of at least -40 or worse beginning as early as the morning of the 8th and lasting as late as the early morning of the 15th. For multiple sites across Prairie County, temperatures below -20 and breezy winds created wind chills of at least -40 or worse beginning in the early morning of the 9th and lasting into the early morning of the 14th. The peak wind chill of -49 was recorded from 2:08 AM to 3:08 AM on the 12th at the Big Sheep Mountain RAWS site (LCFM8).

For multiple sites across eastern Roosevelt County, temperatures below -20 and breezy winds created wind chills of at least -40 or worse beginning in the early morning of the 6th and lasting into the evening of the 13th. The peak wind chill of -49 was recorded from  4:55 AM  to 5:10 AM on the 12th at the Culbertson airport mesonet site.

For multiple sites across Richland County, temperatures below -20 and breezy winds created wind chills of at least -40 or worse beginning as early as the early morning of the 6th and lasting as late as the morning of the 14th. The peak wind chill of -51 was recorded both at 3:54 AM and 6:55 AM on the 12th at the Sioux Pass MT-16 DOT site (MTSOO).

At the Beaver Hill I-94 DOT site (MTBVR), temperatures below -20 and breezy winds created wind chills of at least -40 or worse from the night of the 8th into the morning of the 14th. The peak wind chill of -51 was recorded from 4:33 AM to 6:33 AM on the 12th.

To start the month of March, drought conditions (D2-Severe) retreated from county-wide coverage at the end of February, to be confined only to the western and southern edges of Sheridan County.  For the last two weeks of the month of March, drought conditions (D2-Severe) then expanded again to include all of Sheridan County.

To start the month of March, drought conditions (D2-Severe) from February continued across central and eastern portions of Daniels County (generally near and east of MT Highway 13).  For the last two weeks of March, drought conditions (D2-Severe) then expanded to include all of Daniels County.

In the first week of March, drought conditions (D2-Severe) from February, found across all but the western edge of Western Roosevelt County, expanded to include the southwestern portion of Western Roosevelt County. From the second week of March through the end of the month, drought conditions (D2-Severe) then expanded to include all of Western Roosevelt County.

Drought conditions (D2-Severe) from February persisted across all of Eastern Roosevelt County through the entire month of March. Through the last half of March, drought conditions (D3-Extreme) advanced westward from western North Dakota to enter the southeastern corner of Eastern Roosevelt County.

In the first week of March, drought conditions (D2-Severe) from February, found across all but the southwestern corner of Richland County, expanded to include all of Richland County. Through the last half of March, drought conditions (D3-Extreme) advanced westward from western North Dakota, to spread into a good portion of east-central and northeastern Richland County.

In the first week of March, drought conditions (D2-Severe) from February, found only in the northeast corner of McCone County, spread toward the southwest to cover more than half of the county. From the second week of March through the end of the month, drought conditions (D2-Severe) expanded further to cover all but the western and southwestern edges of McCone County.

In the first week of March, drought conditions (D2-Severe) from February, found across the eastern half of Dawson County, expanded to include all of Dawson County, which continued through the end of the month.
Drought Conditions (D2-Severe) persisted across all of Wibaux County through the entire month of March.

In the first week of March, drought conditions (D2-Severe) from February, found only in the eastern edge of Prairie County, expanded westward to include almost half of the county and persisted there through the end of the month.

To start the month of March drought conditions (D2-Severe) began only in the far southeastern corner of Central and Southern Valley County (the Frazer area).  By the second week of March, drought conditions (D2-Severe) drastically expanded westward to spread across all but the southwestern corner of Central and Southern Valley County, which persisted there through the end of the month.

In the second week of March, drought conditions (D2-Severe) began across the southern and southeastern portions of Northern Valley County.  Then, through the last two weeks of March, drought conditions (D2-Severe) spread across all of Northern Valley County.

In the second week of March, new drought conditions (D2-Severe) began across the eastern portion of Central and Southeastern Phillips County.  Through the last two weeks of March, drought conditions (D2-Severe) spread further westward to cover most of the northeastern third of Central and Southeastern Phillips County.

In the second week of March, drought conditions (D2-Severe) began in the far southeastern corner of Northern Phillips County.  Through the last two weeks of March, drought conditions (D2-Severe) spread across all of Northern Valley County.

At the Navajo MT-5 DOT site (MTRED), sustained winds of at least 40 mph were common at least each hour during the afternoon and evening, and again during the late night.  The peak wind gust of 65 mph was measured at 6:31 PM MST.

At multiple locations across Sheridan County, sustained winds of at least 40 mph were common from the afternoon of the 29th into the early morning of the 30th.  The peak wind gust of 64 mph was recorded at the Plentywood mesonet site from 3:50 PM to 4:48 PM MST.

At multiple locations across Richland County, sustained winds of at least 40 mph were common from the late morning through the late night of the 29th.  The peak wind gust of 63 mph was recorded at the Sioux Pass MT-16 DOT site (MTSOO).

At multiple locations across Richland County, periods of sustained winds of at least 40 mph were occasional from the late morning on the 29th into the afternoon on the 30th, but were mainly focused during the afternoon on the 29th.  The peak wind gust of 67 mph was recorded at 12:45 PM MST at the mesonet site near Hoyt (MTM28).

At the Beaver Hill I-94 DOT site (MTBVR), periods of sustained winds of at least 40 mph were occasional from the morning on the 29th through the afternoon on the 30th, but were mainly focused from the afternoon through the night of the 29th.  Peak wind gusts of 73 mph were recorded multiple times during the afternoon of the 29th.

At the BLM Terry mesonet site (MTM29), sustained winds of at least 40 mph and or gusts of at least 58 mph were common for about four hours during the mid day and afternoon of the 29th.  The peak wind gust of 66 mph was recorded 3:00 PM MST.

At multiple locations across McCone County, sustained winds of at least 40 mph and/or wind gusts of at least 58 mph were measured from mid day into the evening of the 29th. The peak wind gust of 63 mph was recorded at the Cow Creek MT-13 DOT site (MTCOW).

At multiple locations across Garfield County, periods of sustained winds of at least 40 mph and/or wind gusts of at least 58 mph were occasional from the morning through the afternoon on the 29th. The peak wind gusts of 64 mph were recorded multiple times from 10:48 AM to 1:48 PM MST at the Jordan airport ASOS site (KJDN).

At multiple locations across Western Roosevelt County, sustained winds of at least 40 mph were common from mid day into the evening on the 29th, while stronger gusts were more common in the early evening on the 29th. The peak wind gusts of 61 mph were recorded from 5:41 PM to 5:46 PM MST at the McDonalds MT-13 DOT site (MTMCD).

At the Malta airport AWOS site (KM75), periods of sustained winds of at least 40 mph and/or wind gusts of at least 58 mph were occasional from the morning through the afternoon on the 29th. The peak wind gust of 59 mph was recorded at 12:35 PM MST.

At multiple sites in Southwestern Phillips County, periods of sustained winds of at least 40 mph and/or wind gusts of at least 58 mph were occasional from the early morning on the 29th into the early morning on the 30th, but were mainly focused from the late morning through the afternoon of the 29th. At the Bluff Creek RAWS site (BLUM8), all sustained winds were less than 40 mph, but a single peak wind gust of 59 mph was recorded at 4:44 PM MST.

At multiple sites in Central and Southern Valley County, periods of sustained winds of at least 40 mph and/or wind gusts of at least 58 mph were occasional from the morning into the afternoon on the 29th. To start the month of April in Sheridan County, ongoing drought conditions (D2-Severe) worsened to D3-Extreme across the entire county, which persisted through the end of April.

To start the month of April, ongoing drought conditions (D3-Extreme) in the far southeast corner of Eastern Roosevelt county and D2-Severe drought everywhere else, worsened to fill all of Eastern Roosevelt County with D3-Extreme drought, which persisted there through the end of April.

To start the month of April, ongoing drought conditions (D3-Extreme) in the northeast corner of Richland County and D2-Severe everywhere else, worsened to spread D3-Extreme drought to all but the northwest corner of the county. During the last week of April, D3-Extreme drought had spread to cover the entire county.

To start the month of April, ongoing drought conditions (D2-Severe), worsened to D3-Extreme for all but the southwest corner of Wibaux County.  By mid-April, D3-Extreme drought had spread to all of the county, which persisted through the end of the month.

To start the month of April, ongoing drought conditions (D2-Severe), worsened to D3-Extreme along the far eastern edge of Daniels County.  In the second week of April, D3-Extreme drought spread westward through the eastern half of the county.  By the last week of April, D3-Extreme drought had spread through all of the county, which persisted through the end of the month.

To start the month of April, ongoing drought conditions (D2-Severe), worsened to D3-Extreme in eastern and northeastern portions of Western Roosevelt County.  By the last week of April, D3-Extreme drought had spread westward through all of Western Roosevelt County, which persisted through the end of the month.

To start the month of April, ongoing drought conditions (D2-Severe) for all but the southwestern portion of McCone County, now worsened to D3-Extreme drought in the far southeastern corner of the county.  In the third week of April, D2-Severe drought had filled in the southwestern portions of the county, and D3-Extreme drought spread further through more of southeastern McCone County.  By the last week of April, D3-Extreme drought had spread through the eastern half of the county, which persisted through the end of the month.

To start the month of April in Dawson County, ongoing drought conditions (D2-Severe) worsened to D3-Extreme drought for all but the far northwest, southwest, and southeast corners of the county.  By the third week of April, D3-Extreme drought had spread to all but the far northwest corner of the county. By the last week of April, D3-Extreme drought had spread through all of Dawson County, which persisted through the end of the month.

To start the month of April, ongoing drought conditions (D2-Severe) from the northeastern half of Prairie County, had spread into all but the western edge of the county.  By the third week of April, D2-Severe drought had filled in the western edge, and the remainder of the county had worsened into D3-Extreme drought, which persisted through the end of the month.

Ongoing drought conditions (D2-Severe) through all of Northern Valley County remained through the first week of April.  By the second week of April, the western two-thirds of Northern Valley County worsened into D3-Extreme drought.  By the last week of April, all of Northern Valley County worsened into D3-Extreme drought, which persisted through the end of the month.

Ongoing drought conditions (D2-Severe) through all but the southwestern corner of Central and Southern Valley County continued through the first week of April. By the second week of April, the central to northwestern section of Central and Southern Valley County worsened into D3-Extreme drought. By the third week, D2-Severe drought filled in the southwestern corner.  By the last week of April, D-3 Extreme drought filled in the central and eastern section of Central and Southern Valley County (basically all areas near and north of US Highway 2).

By the third week of April, and persisting through the end of the month, drought conditions (D2-Severe) drastically expanded westward to spread across all but the southeastern corner of Garfield County.

By the third week of April, and persisting through the end of the month, drought conditions (D2-Severe) drastically expanded westward to spread across all but the southwestern corner of Petroleum County.

Ongoing drought conditions (D2-Severe) through all of Northern Phillips County remained through the first week of April. By the second week of April, the eastern two-thirds of Northern Phillips County worsened into D3-Extreme drought, which persisted through the end of the month.

Ongoing drought conditions (D2-Severe) over the northeastern third of Central and Southeastern Phillips County remained through the first week of April. By the second week of April, the far northeastern portion of Central and Southeastern Phillips County worsened into D3-Extreme drought. By the third week, D2-Severe drought had expanded into western and southern portions. By the last week of April, D-2 Severe drought expanded into the far northwestern portions of Central and southeast Phillips County.

Ongoing drought conditions (D3-Extreme) continued across all of Western Roosevelt County through the entire month of May.

Ongoing drought conditions (D3-Extreme) continued across all of Sheridan County through the entire month of June.

Ongoing drought conditions (D3-Extreme) across all of Daniels County at the beginning of June, improved slightly to D2-Severe in the far southwest corner of the county.  By mid month and through the end of June, D2-Severe drought replaced D3-Extreme drought through the west-central portion of the county.
Ongoing drought conditions (D3-Extreme) continued across all of Eastern Roosevelt County through the entire month of June.

Ongoing drought conditions (D3-Extreme) across all of Richland County to begin the month of June, got some relief in the second week as D2-Severe drought replaced D3-Extreme drought across western and central portions of the county and in the third week in the far southeast corner of the county.  Drought conditions then remained that way through the end of the month.

Ongoing drought conditions (D3-Extreme) across all of Dawson County to begin the month of June, got some relief in the second week as D2-Severe drought replaced D3-Extreme drought over the northwest third of the county and remained that way through the end of the month.

Ongoing drought conditions (D3-Extreme) across all of Wibaux County to begin the month of June, got some small relief in the third week as D2-Severe drought replaced D3-Extreme drought in the far northeast corner of the county and remained that way through the end of the month.

Ongoing drought conditions (D3-Extreme) for all of Prairie County except the southwest corner in D2-Severe to start the month of June, showed a little improvement with the northwest corner also in D2-Severe by the second week. These conditions then continued this way through the end of the month.

Ongoing drought conditions (D3-Extreme) for all of Western Roosevelt county to start the month of June improved slightly to D2-Severe for the western third of Western Roosevelt County by the second week, which continued this way through the end of the month.

Ongoing drought conditions for all of McCone County were D3-Extreme except the far southwest edge in D2-Severe to start the month of June. By the second week, D2-Severe prevailed across all of McCone county, but the far southeastern corner of the county remained in D3-Extreme. For the last few weeks of the month, D3-Extreme returned to the northwest corner of the county.

Ongoing drought conditions (D3-Extreme) across all of Northern Valley County at the beginning of June, changed very little in the second week with D2-Severe in the far southeast corner of Northern Valley County. These conditions then continued this way through the end of the month.

To start the month of June, ongoing drought conditions (D3-Extreme) were across most of Central and Southern Valley with D2-Severe in the southwestern portion. By the second week, D2-Severe prevailed across most of Central and Southern Valley County with D3-Extreme in the northwest portion. By the fourth week, D3-Extreme drought returned to most areas, while D2-Severe remained over the eastern edge.

To start the month of June, ongoing drought conditions (D2-Severe) were across all but the southeastern edge of Garfield County while D3-Extreme remained in the far northeastern corner of the county (Haxby Point).  By the second week, D3-Extreme retreated eastward to leave all but the southeastern edge of Garfield County in D2-Severe.  By the third week of the month, D3-Extreme returned to central and northern portions of the county. By the end of the month, D3-Extreme spread further west to include most of Garfield county, except the southeast now in D2-Severe.

Ongoing drought conditions (D2-Severe) in the western third of Northern Phillips County, and D3-Extreme drought in the eastern two thirds of Northern Phillips County continued through the entire month of June.

Ongoing drought conditions (D3-Extreme) in the far northeastern portion of Central and Southeastern Phillips County and D2-Severe over the remainder of Central and Southeastern Phillips County persisted through the first half of the month of June.  By the third week, D3-Extreme drought extended southward to cover a bit more of the eastern edge of Central and Southeastern Phillips County.  By the end of the month D3-Extreme has spread to more of the eastern and southern sections with D2-Severe holding on over western and northwestern sections.

Ongoing drought conditions (D2-Severe) across all of Petroleum County prevailed through the first three weeks of the month of June. By the end of the month, D3-Extreme drought had spread over all of Petroleum County.

Thus far through the entire spring and early summer season, this area only experienced up to D1-Moderate drought, but by the third week of June, D2-Severe drought had spread through the Little Rocky Mountains, and remained there through the end of the month.

Ongoing drought conditions (D3-Extreme) in Sheridan County improved slightly to D2-Severe in the second week of July for most of the county, with the exception of the extreme southwest portion of Sheridan County which remained in D3-Extreme drought.  These conditions then continued through the remainder of the month of July.

To start the month of July, ongoing drought conditions (D3-Extreme) were across the eastern two thirds and the far northwest corner of Daniels County, and the western third of the county was in D2-Severe drought.  In the second week, for the eastern portions, D3-Extreme drought retreated to south-central and southeastern portions of the county.  These conditions then continued through the rest of the month.

To start the month of July, ongoing drought conditions (D3-Extreme) were in place across all of Eastern Roosevelt County.  In the second week, the far eastern portion near the state line improved to D2-Severe.  In the third week, the far southeastern portion returned to D3-Extreme drought.  These conditions then continued through the end of the month.
Ongoing drought conditions (D2-Severe) were in the western half and the far southeastern corner of Richland County, with D3-Extreme drought elsewhere.  These conditions lasted through all of July.

To start out July, (D2-Severe) drought was located over the northwest third of the county and (D3-Extreme) drought was located in the southeastern two thirds of the county.  These conditions remained this way through the entire month of July with no changes.

All but the extreme northeast corner of Wibaux County was in (D3-Extreme) drought conditions with the extreme northeast corner being in (D2-Severe) drought.  These conditions remained unchanged throughout the whole month of July.

Ongoing drought conditions (D3-Extreme) continued for the eastern three quarters of Prairie County with (D2-Severe) in the western quarter of the county. These conditions remained unchanged throughout the month of July.

Ongoing drought conditions (D3-Extreme) continued for the eastern two thirds of Western Roosevelt county and (D2-Severe) for the western third of Western Roosevelt County.  These conditions remained unchanged throughout the month of July.

Ongoing drought conditions for McCone County were (D2-Severe) for the majority of the county, the exception being the far northwestern and far southeastern corners where (D3-Extreme) was occurring.  These conditions remained unchanged throughout the month of July.

Ongoing drought conditions (D3-Extreme) occurred across most of Northern Valley County at the beginning of July, the exception being (D2-Severe) in the far southeast corner of Northern Valley County. These conditions remained unchanged throughout the month of July.

To start the month of July, ongoing drought conditions (D3-Extreme) were across most of Central and Southern Valley County with (D2-Severe) in the far eastern portion. By the third week, the western third of Central and Southern Valley County had worsened to (D4-Exceptional Drought) with the middle third remaining in (D3-Extreme) conditions and the eastern third remaining in (D2-Severe) conditions through the end of the month.

Ongoing drought conditions to start July were in (D3-Extreme) across all but the southeastern corner of Garfield County which was in (D2-Severe).  On the third week of July conditions across the northwestern corner worsened to (D4-Exceptional) with (D3-Extreme) remaining across most of central and southwestern Garfield County and (D2-Severe) remaining in the southeastern corner through the end of the month.

Ongoing drought conditions started July as (D2-Severe) in the western third of Northern Phillips County, and (D3-Extreme) drought in the eastern two thirds of Northern Phillips County.  During the second week of July these conditions worsened to (D3-Extreme) for all but the extreme northwest corner of Northern Phillips county which remained in (D2-Severe).  Conditions remained this way through the end of July.

Ongoing drought conditions (D3-Extreme) were in the eastern and southern sections of Central and Southeast Phillips County with D2-Severe over western and northwestern sections.  During the second week of July (D3-Extreme) conditions pushed west with only the far southwestern tip of Central and Southeast Phillips County remaining in (D2-Severe) conditions.  During the third week of July eastern sections of Central and Southeast Phillips County worsened into (D4-Exceptional) conditions.  On the last week the far southwestern tip of Central and Southeast Phillips County worsened into (D3-Extreme) conditions.

Ongoing drought conditions started July with (D3-Extreme) drought across all of Petroleum County.  By week three, the central part of Petroleum County had worsened to (D4-Exceptional) drought with the northern and southern parts of Petroleum County remaining in (D3-Extreme) conditions through the rest of July.

Ongoing drought conditions (D2-Severe) were in the Little Rockies to start the month. During week two, a sliver of (D3-Extreme) moved into northern and west central Little Rockies with (D2-Severe) remaining elsewhere.  On the last week of July most of the Little Rockies worsened into (D3-Extreme) conditions, the exception being the far western corner which remained in (D2-Severe) conditions.
